On section 4-application for water for purposes having precedence affecting prior grants.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Perhaps I should explain this clause more fully. Section 10 has four subsections, and this amendment proposes another subsection (4A). The first subsection declares that any water the property of which is vested in the Crown may be acquired for domestic, municipal, industrial, irrigation, and other purposes, including the granting of permission to erect dams, piers, booms and other necessary works in any non-navigable stream to facilitate the passage of logs, timber and other products of the forest along such stream, upon application being made; secondly, that all applications shall be made in accordance with the provisions of the Act; thirdly, such applications must show precedence according to the respective dates of their filing with the Commission. The fourth subsection provides that, subject to the provisions of subsection 3, applications for the several purposes mentioned shall show precedence in the following order: First, domestic purposes; second, municipal purposes; third, industrial purposes; fourth, irrigation purposes; and fifth, other purposes. That is to say, if there is just ' enough water for necessary domestic purposes, then the minister is bound to give those purposes priority. Then, if there is any more water he is bound to consider municipal purposes; next, industrial purposes, and then irrigation purposes, and finally other purposes. After the lapse of many years and very considerable development of irrigation in Alberta, water rights that have been granted for irrigation purposes or, say, industrial purposes have been exploited, and then perhaps a town springs up, and it turns out that the water is needed for domestic purposes. But the water right has gone and there is no provision for recovering it. So that the clause sought to be added is to give the right to
expropriate water for an inferior purpose for the benefit of a superior purpose upon payment of due compensation.
Mr. MoMASTER: Are these water rights alienated absolutely or only for a term of years?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They are not alienated absolutely. The water right is granted, but I do not think that any definite number of years is fixed. Perhaps the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Buchanan) would know.
I do not think there is a definite period.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The water right is granted subject to certain conditions which must be lived up to year by year, but there is no definite number of years. You could not do that. For example, if you give a water right at the Bow river for irrigation, no man would put in an irrigation system like that of the Northwest Irrigation Company, going to the expense of building a system of canals, as they have done, at a cost of over $12,000,000, unless the water right is perpetuated. As I say, certain conditions contained in the water right must be lived up to, and those conditions are set out in the Irrigation Act; but so long as they comply with those conditions they have a permanent water right.

A number of irrigation systems have developed all oveT Alberta and all have been established by private companies. The Canadian Pacific own what is known as the old company headed by the late Sir Alexander Galt. They secured the rights to irrigate certain lands and in disposing of the lands to the people who purchase from them they have to guarantee a certain amount of water each season. Consequently these water rights, in my judgment, are permanent for all time, because it is part of the contract between the company and the purchasers to supply their land with water. If they cannolt carry out that contract and supply them with water the farm is not worth while and the farmer is stranded. There is a very serious condition in a section of Alberta at this momenlt and there is an urgent demand for the extension of irrigation. In one section of Southern Alberta, stretching from McLeod to Ithe Little Bow river and north thirty miles, the crop was practically blown out last week. Soil drifting is the great trouble there and they feel that the only remedy for the situation is the encouragement and development of irriga-

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext: tion. If the extension of irrigation does not come immediately I venture to say to this House that there will be a movement of hundreds of farmers out of Ithat section of country because under present conditions they cannot farm there with success. Alongside of them there are these irrigation distridts which we have been referring to, where farmers are enjoying ' the greatest ' prosperity, because conditions which strike the man on Ithe dry land do not strike the man on irrigated land.
Dry territory does not help ?

I am sure that an
investment in irrigation on the part of the Albedta Government or of this Government for the purpose of irrigating these lands will save these people to this country and if that investment is not made these people are going Ito leave Canada and they are going to give a black eye to Canada because what they say will not apply to one section only but to the whole of Western Canada. Irrigation has been a huge success in Alberta and Ithe yields of irrigated land are much greater than those of dry land in any part of Western Canada. Last year in the irrigated district alongside the city of Lelthbridge the wealth in crops raised was about $5,000,000. The minister will bear me out in the statement that he travelled over eighty miles otf country there laslt fall and that he did not see the slightest indication of a crop until he reached this irrigated disltrict. It was rich with all kinds of crops. If we can do something to encourage irrigation and to establish these systems it will keep the people already in that country, and for the Governmenlts which are responsible for bringing them into Canada and settling them on this land it will be a good investment because any money expended in order to establish a system of irrigation will be returned, I venture to say, a hundred fold.

May I just remark
that the object of my question to the minister was to bring before the committee the inadvisability of alienating the public domain where it is possible to carry on the development without doing so. I can quite understand how difficult it may be to get an irrigation company to make a great capital investment without giving them a tenure which is going to repay them and keep matters in a condition of practical continuity or permanency. I would be glad to learn from the minister whether, when

these rights are granted, provision is made for an increase in the tolls for the water. Let me draw attention to a similar case. In the province of Quebec we have a very valuable Crown domain in our forests. These forests are operated by lumbermen who have great investments in their mills, slides, booms, improvements of waterways and so on. But the Government, about every ten years, adjusts the scale of stump-age and usually on an ascending scale. I would be glad to know whether the conditions under which this water is leased to irrigation companies contains provisions whereby, when the water becomes more and more valuable owing to the increase in population and the fertility of the soil, the people will be able to draw the benefit from that by charging a higher rate.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not think there is any provision for a rate for the water at all. That is the recollection also of my hon. friend from Lethbridge (Mr. Buchanan). In this connection-I do not say it as a rejoinder-the water rights that have been granted, I think, were granted some time before 1911 to the Canada Land Irrigation Company and the Canadian Pacific. The great bulk of the development had proceeded through water rights granted before that year; so that if there was an error in policy it would not be attributable to me or to the two ministers before me. I do not think there was; I think the policy was right. The water which is used I have never regarded as something out of which the rest of the Dominion could exact a toll. It should be used with the greatest advantage to the people within the radius who can use it. All we seek to do is to so conserve and distribute the surplus water supply of that country as to get the utmost possible benefit for the -people there. We give water rights to companies for irrigation purposes providing municipal and industrial purposes do not first appear as necessary. We give the right, say, to take so many second feet from the St. Mary river. We do not give that right until we see what is going to be done with the water, what is [DOT] the plan for diverting that water and storing it and what land is to be benefited by it. We look after that. We also see that we have control of the water rate to be charged. We control also the duty of water; that is to say the amount of water that can be supplied to any given acreage of land per year. The Dominion Government will not permit the issue of water leases by the companies. The Canadian Pacific and the Canada Land and Irrigation Company-they are the chief ones-use only

the form of lease that is approved by the department. In the body of these leases provision is made for duty of water; consequently, we control the duty of water. We control the rate to be charged and everything else but the object is not to get revenue for the Dominion. The object is to get the utmost value of the water.
I want to say a word in reference to the hon. member for Lethbridge. I quite understand his bringing this question before the committee. Among the projects that have been before the Irrigation Branch of the Department of the Interior one of the most important is that of the Lethbridge Northern Irrigation project. Let the committee understand that the policy of the Department of the Interior, historically and most clearly emphasized within recent years, has been to only perform such services as are necessary to be performed in order that the department may know what the best use of the water is and in order that the department may have all the engineering and survey information to enable it to administer the water rights of 'the country. Consequently all the survey work has been done by the Interior Department. We also have offered-looking to the same end-to lend engineering assistance to any practical construction enterprise; but beyond that the Interior Department, or the Government of Canada, has never gone. We have taken the ground that after that work is done and the money expended for that purpose -from the Federal Treasury is gone-and it has amounted to huge sums of money; I think our appropriation this year is in the neighbourhood of a million-after granting very large sums of money-and they are not returnable; this is not in the nature of a loan, it is in the nature of an investment out of the Federal Treasury for the benefit of the district-then we feei that our duty is performed and beyond that point the obligation rests upon the local authorities, municipal or provincial, or even private.
Now, one of the areas in which we have operated for some time and in respect of which our work is practically complete- it is largely advanced anyway-is this northern Lethbridge irrigation district. That district has been without water, has been scourged with famine for three years previous to this, and consequently distress-or something very close to distress-prevails throughout it. Some 90,000 acres are included in our irrigation project there. This year-although generally speaking the season was propitious and there was quite a
lot of rain-a tornado has swept the district and has driven the soil into piles; in .fact it has denuded the whole surface of the earth in that district, of soil.
Mr. MoMAiSTER:	The people should
come back to the East.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: This could not have occurred had the actual work been done. .That fs to say had the land been brought under irrigation there could have been no such drifting of the soil. Therefore at the present time a very serious situation faces those people, and I can understand the concern of the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Buchanan) in this regard. Now so far as the Government of Canada is concerned I do not know that all of us feel the same intimate sympathy with the people that I do. I would feel like going to the extreme limit that the Federal Government could possibly go, in justice to the rest of this Dominion in seeking to cooperate with the provincial authorities to relieve that situation; but I think the line having been clearly drawn, and there being no possibility of doubt as to the wisdom of the point at which it is drawn, we cannot go further-at least until we have some proposal from the local authorities looking for further advance.

I would like to represent the view of the people in that particular community. They feel that the condition which exists this year should be treated as an emergency because it has left them in practically the same position as Halifax was left in a few years ago, when that city was blown up. Practically everything in the world that these people had has been blown away. Now I make this statement: They have had crop failures there for three years, and everything they have is mortgaged up to the hilt. There is no relief for them whatever except through the development of irrigation. That will save them and that will make the district-and the people who live in that district-worth while to this country. If they are not saved now it is hard to say what will happen. The chief trouble is to dispose of the bonds and-in my judgment-there will have to be co-operation between the province and the Dominion in order to met the situation. If the leader of the Opposition or the member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) should happen to visit the West this year and go into my part of the country I will show them some of the richest country in Western 'Canada-that is the irrigation sections around Lethbridge.

I will be very glad to see both gentlemen and to show those sections to them.
4p.m. Mr. MACKENZIE KING:	We
will be there.
Mr. MeKENZTE: I have not very much to say about this matter. I am in the fullest possible sympathy with the people whose lands have been placed in the condition described by the Minister of the Interior, and the hon. member for Lethbridge. The latter said that the farmers in that part of the country are in the same position as the people of Halifax when they had the explosion. There is this difference, ho-wever, in the two situations: The people of the Lethbridge district have to find fault with the dispensation of Providence, whereas the people of Halifax had to suffer by reason of the stupidity of certain men sent by the Federal Government to take over Halifax harbour. There is that very strong difference between the two situations.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
What does the hon.
gentleman say?

I said that the farmers in that section of the West have to put up with the dispensation of Providence,-with hot winds, tornadoes, and that sort of thing -whereas the people of Halifax had to find fault with a lot of stupid men sent by this Government to handle the business of the harbour. That is the striking difference between the two situations.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Does the hon. member mean to say that that caused the explosion at Halifax?

Yes, that caused the
explosion. The finding of the court was that the ships were stupidly handled, allowed to come into collision, and that caused the explosion.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Did we handle the
ships?

Your officers handled
the ships.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I thought they were
handled by their captains?

Certainly, but they
were under the guidance of the harbour master at the time. He was an official of this Government, and if he knew his business would not have allowed the two ships to come together at the narrow place where they collided. That is certainly where he was at fault. I believe possibly the captains did the best they could, but the vessels should never have been allowed to

come together in a narrow passage when the harbour authorities could and should have prevented it. There is that striking difference between the situation in the West and the situation in the harbour of Halifax. But what I was going to say to the minister is that if we as a Government, and as a country, are selling those lands-[DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Is the hon. member
sure that the Government is not responsible for that tornado in the West? I would not like him to be too rash.
Mr. MeMASTEF.: He said you were not responsible.

Unless the hon. gentleman unites himself with Providence, I leave that matter in doubt for the present. What I was going on to say is this: If we as a Government, and as a country, encouraged people to go upon this land we certainly have every right to look after them and see that everything is done for them that possibly could be done. But if those lands were sold by land companies and speculators, as a matter of speculation I do not quite see the justice of our coming in at very large expense and helping to make those lands habitable, when I am hopeful we have other lands better fitted for cultivation which ought to have been available for settlement. The point I make is that if we are encouraging farmers to settle on lands in the West we should first of all place them on good lands, if we have anything at all to say about it, which would offer a better prospect to settlers and entail less expense upon the people of the country. I say further that if lands that were 'being held for speculative reasons were sold to farmers for farming purposes when they were not fit for such purposes then those companies and speculators and not the people of 'Canada should assume the responsibility. Such land companies have no very great claim on us to make those lands fit for cultivation as farms when they were not suitable for any such purpose at the time of sale. I draw a distinction between the two conditions. I repeat that if we encourage settlers to go on those lands, and place them there, we have a right to do everything possible to help them out. But if the lands were bought from land companies who were holding the land for speculative purposes then the sufferers should look to those companies for succour in their time of distress; I do not think they have the same claim on us, as they might have under the other conditions referred to. If we have lands which are fit

for cultivation and which do not need irrigation we should direct people to those lands before we put them on lands which are not fit for cultivation.

The people who are
crying for irrigation and who must have it to save their lives are people who have been in that district for fifteen years. They have their homes and their farm buildings, but they are stranded now because they can get no crops on account of the peculiar situation that exists. They are prepared to bond everything they have, land, buildings and everything else, in order to raise money to bring irrigation into that district. There is practically no wild or idle land in that part of the country-that is to say, that would be of advantage to promoters or companies. The district has been incorporated under the Alberta Irrigation Act, but it is impossible except at great sacrifice to dispose of the bonds on the financial market at the present time; their disposition under these conditions would increase the cost per acre for irrigation. So that if in some way Governments could assist to maintain the value of these bonds it would be well worth while. Mention was made by my hon. friend (Mr. McMaster) of charges for water. In the commencement of development of irrigation in Western Canada, as I recollect it, Governments were only too willing to encourage companies to go in and irrigate the land, and to give them certain privileges in regard to water. But in no case can any of these companies make a charge for the water right to the individual farmer without first obtaining the approval of the Department of Irrigation at Ottawa. There is no opportunity for them to use the water in order to make money out of it for themselves. The matter is dealt with somewhat on the same basis as the distribution of Hydro-Electric power and light in Ontario. That was the policy that was adopted back in the early nineties and which has been followed since. The district I speak of has been formed practically on the same basis as a rural municipality and the people have voted a bond issue in order to bring in the water for distribution over that area. As I have said, if they could dispose of these bonds there would be no trouble whatever, but at present they cannot dispose of them. A wind storm has come along and blown all their crop away and they are stranded. What I now want is co-operation between the Dominion and Provincial Governments to bring about a solution of the problem.
Did I understand my hon. friend (Mr. McKenzie) to blame the harbour master at Halifax for the explosion that took place there?

Not the man who is
really called the harbour master, because he was superseded by the officer who was in charge at that time.
I wish to say that he had nothing to do with it. It was taken out of his hands altogether by the naval authorities.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 5-power to reserve any unappropriated water, and allocate the whole or any part in the public interest:

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Will the minister explain this clause?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
When I was looking
over this coal area last August accompanied by Mr. Drake, we came to the conclusion that the supply of water that was going to be available would be far short of what could be usefully applied to the land there and that if priority of application were in the future to prevail we were not likely to get the best results from that water. Consequently I put through an Order in Council, which at the time we felt was fully within our powers, reserving the unappropriated water in order that a full survey might be made of it with a view to its best utilization. This clause grants that power and dates it back to the date of the order so that there may be no question as to the validity of the reservation then made.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 6-storage of water:

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
This clause provides
for the joint utilization of works constructed or under construction and for their joint maintenance thereafter. The principle was embodied in the old legislation but the old legislation enabled only the division or use of works constructed. This goes on and in more detail provides that during construction the minister may make orders as to joint utilization, say, of a canal, or of a reservoir, upon such terms as may be mutually agreed upon or, failing agreement, as determined by himself. Otherwise duplication would inevitably result in capital investment in canal, reservoir and irrigation construction.
Mr. McMAiSTER: Subclause (2) of clause 6 reads:

The minister may grant to any applicant for the carriage of water to his lands, the right to use any portion of the works constructed, under construction, or to be constructed, by any company whenever, In his opinion, it is necessary or desirable so to do.
The word "company," it seems to me, contemplates that only a company is to put up works of this character. I would presume they were generally put up by companies, but I could quite understand where a rich man interested in the development of a section might himself as an individual be constructing works. In that case, it would seem to me that a neighbour would have the same right to come in as if the work were being constructed by a company. I would, therefore, suggest to the minister the use of some language which would cover both a private individual and a company or a partnership.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I did not notice that. I do not know why the word "company" is used, and unless the word "company" is defined in the interpretation clauses of the main Act to include a person, I would certainly think it should be changed. I should not like to change it now because I have not the main Act in front of me, but unless the word "company" is defined so as to .be wide enough, I will ask that an amendment to that effect he made in the Senate.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 7-penalty for refusal to neglect to carry out orders.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: This clause is of the nature of several others to which I have taken objection, namely, giving the minister power to issue orders and then providing penalties of a somewhat severe nature should ady one disobey them. When penalties are provided, some safeguard and protection ought to be thrown around the liberties of individuals, and the power to make orders enforcable by penalty ought to be restricted at least to an Order in Council and not simply left to the caprice of the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The minister has to do what is set out, say in the previous clause; he has to come to a conclusion as to what is a reasonable arrangement for the use and maintenance of a joint canal, and he determines on that. It is necessary that his order be obeyed; otherwise the clause is nugatory. I only wish to ,say again that I have no objection and I have never known of any minister who has had any objection to being compelled to go to Council for an Order. That is a protection to the minister; he feels that the responsibility is not

his. The difficulty is that the proceeding cannot be anything other than a mere formality, and indeed, an impediment to the proper transaction of business that is necessarily the business of Government. The present state of affairs is really ridiculous; a minister cannot accept the resignation of a clerk; he cannot enfranchise an Indian on his own application; h;e cannot cancel a sale of .school lands except by an Order of the Governor in Council, and what is the result? Every week there may be twenty school land sales cancelled, I do not know how many Indians enfranchised and all the rest of it. I have given only a few illustrations out of hundreds. The consequence is that a plethora of material reaches Council, and the consideration of subjects that must be considered by the Cabinet as a whole is really impeded by the Cabinet having to go through whaJt is merely routine, and you get no result from that at all. I know this seems o.f itself as important, and unless one realizes the tremendous scope and extent of the volume of business that comes before Council, one is very much inclined to do this. I have not the silghteslt exception to this being done; but I know as well as I am standing on my feet that it would not be ultimately in the public interest. Of course, if we change this, we shall have to go back and change all the other clauses of the Bill.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Might I point out to the minister thalt there is a considerable difference between the acceptance of the resignation of some clerk by Order in Council and the imposing of a penalty of $500 or two months imprisonment upon a free citizen? That is the point to which I am taking exception. I quite agree with what the minister has said that the time of Council is altogether too much taken up in dealing with routine matters that come before it; but there are some matters concerning which it is really wise to have extra precautions taken and any matter [DOT]which imposes a penalty upon an individual belongs Ito that class. The minister is right when he says that Ithis would be a protection to the minister himself. In these cases, many orders must necessarily be left to subordinate officials, the minister simply giving his signature of approval to an order. If a little extra precaution could be thrown around all orders of that kind, a greater sense of security would be afforded to parties concerned, and I hope the minister 'will follow out the suggestion.

Mr, MEIGHEN:	I would be glad Ito do
so and to go over the Bill and change every clause of it so as to have every order made by the minister supplemented by an Order in Council. But I feel, if I do that, I shall have-to go through the whole of the original Adt which I think was passed by a former Government of the party to which the hon. member belongs, and see that the minister had no power to make an order there except wilth the authority of the Governor in Council. As long as the minister has power to make an order, there must be a clause providing for a penalty. It happens that there are several specific clauses providing for penalties for specific violations ; bult through some oversight there was no general clause, as there always should be, providing for a penalty for violation of the Act. This is that general clause, and consequently it applies to the whole Act. If the minister is not to be allowed to make an order for himself, then the whole Act must be amended so as to ensure that he has not that power. There is no use giving the minister the power to make an order and then having no clause which enables that order to be enforced. That prevents me from accepting the suggestion, although I would much rather accept it as regards this Bill than have any contention over it.

Might I make a suggestion which might help the situation, although perhaps I am not sufficiently familiar with the Bill or with the original Act to make this suggestion with any degree of confidence? The minister will not be in the position of having to fine or imprison a person unless that person has refused to obey the minister's order, and these orders will very possibly come under section 6. If I am right so far, I would suggest that under subsection (3) of section 6 the minister is the sole arbiter to determine the amount to be paid. Why not provide for an appeal from the minister's decision, either to a court or to Council, so that those people who are not satisfied with the minister's decision shall have the right to appeal. Then if people have not confidence in their case and are not prepared to appeal, they cannot complain if the minister is given power to punish them for their recalcitrancy.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I think it would be better and would meet the hon. member's wishes if we amended section 6 to make every order of the minister subject to the approval of the Governor in Council. Then
any one disobeying section 6 would be disobeying the Governor in Council. So far as section 6 is concerned, I am quite prepared to have those words inserted.

I do not desire to accumulate the work before Council. I quite understand the soundness of the minister's contention that Council is already loaded up with a lot of routine matters to the disadvantage of the public interest. My idea was to give to a party dissatisfied with the minister's determination of the question an opportunity to appeal to Council or to the court of appeal in the province in which the dispute arose. Then if the man did not take an appeal he would be acquiescing in the minister's judgment, and he could not complain of receiving his punishment at the hands of the minister, while it would protect the subject from having the minister alone find him guilty or render a decision with which he was dissatisfied. The minister is going even further to meet my objection than I asked. I limited my demand, in view of his statement as to the accumulation of routine matters before Council.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
If the minister has power to make an order and makes an order, you could not say to a man "If you dispute that order we will give you an appeal against the minister to the Governor in Council, "because the Governor in Council would be bound to support the minister or the minister would have to go. Once the order goes out, that is the law of the land, and the only place to bring in the Governor in Council is precedent to the order going out.
Mr. MdMASTER: It seems to me that the minister under subsection (3) of section G really sits as an arbitrator, or a sort of judge, and there is no reason, it seems to me, why sitting as a judge he should feel that he would have to resign if Council did not support him.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Once his order has gone out. The minister makes his order determining the conditions for the joint use of the canal. His order has gone out. Then John Smith says: "I will not follow it. I will not pay my share," and he goes to the Governor in Council. Now the minister's order is the law of the land. It has gone out, and John Smith is appealing between the minister and the Government, and the Government must support its own minister. There is no precedent anywhere for an appeal of that kind. I am quite content to

say that no such order shall go out until the Governor in Council approves of it. Certainly I agree with the leader of the Opposition that there are many other things of infinitely less consequence that the Governor in Council must approve of.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Will the minister submit his amendment?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I will prepare it while the Chairman is reading the next section.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On the motion of Mr. Meighen the committee reverted to section 6-storage of water:

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I beg to add as subclause 5 of section 6 the following:
All orders made under this section shall be approved by the Governor in Council.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
That is all
right.
Amendment .agreed to.

stagedirection
speechtext:
House again in Committee of Supply, Mr. Boivin in the Chair:
Militia and Defence-Cadet services, $390,000.

speakerposition: subtopic
speechtext:

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: There is a considerable increase here over the amount that was voted last year for this purpose. Perhaps the minister would give the committee some particulars as to what he proposes to do with this money.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
The amount voted for
19-19-20 was $100,000; this year it is $390,000. During the year 1918-19 the expenditure under this head was only $68,000, but in 1913-14, the year immediately preceding the war, it was $392,206. That was considered about the normal expenditure for pre-war times. During the war not so much attention wae paid to cadet training as prior to the war, hut I think the House will realize the value of that training. It has a value to the whole country apart altogether from any question of militia training, and it is proposed now to return to the pre-war basis, the amount asked for the current year being practically the same as was voted before the war. During the war certain reductions were made and the annual cadet camps were not held. It is intended to hold those camps this year, and to restore the former allowances which 
were made to the instructors. It is the purpose to give school teachers and instructors the opportunity of themselves being trained for the purpose of properly instructing the cadets. In this way the pre-war system will be re-instated.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
What classes
of persons are given cadet training?
.Mr. GUTHRIE: The Statute that applies to this subject is the Militia Act, Section 64, the Statutes of Canada, 1906. The cadet corps are divided into three classes: first, those composed of pupils in attendance at colleges and schools controlled by the Government of the province in which such institutions are situated; second, those composed of pupils in attendance at colleges and schools not under government control; and third, those composed of lads who, with the permission of their parents or guardians, prefer to join a corps unconnected with any educational establishment. Those three classes are trained.
What formalities are necessary for the formation of a cadet corps in any rural district?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Application is made to cadet training inspector of the district asking for permission to establish a corps and setting out the number of pupils that can be entered and trained. If the number is sufficient to warrant its formation, the corps is immediately established and a man is sent from the military district to undertake its training. Once the corps is established it is entitled to all the benefits that accrue under the Act, and teachers are entitled to a certain amount of military training, if you choose to term it so, in order to qualify them for the work in their district.
Mr. 'MARCH: What accoutrement does the department furnish?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
The accoutrement is
modest. The drill inspector is paid, but for the cadets themselves there is only an allowance of $1.25,-$1 for uniform and 25 cents for a hat. I think that is the only accoutrement allowance, although I am not sure of that. Possibly in many cases we have supplied some obsolete arms for the purpose of infantry drill, but the only actual allowance for uniform is $1.25 per head.
Are the camps held during July and August?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
As a rule they are held in August and they last for six days. The Estimate for the present year, based on that

of the year preceding the war, is made up as follows: subsistence for 25,000 cadets in camp at 50c. each day, $75,000; transportation and return at $3 per head, $75,000; washing blankets after camp, $5,000; staffs at cadet camps, $10,000; and the usual grant to the Canadian Rifle League of $500. That grant is for cadets. I have given the cost of the camps.

I suppose it is rather
a dangerous thing for a person to say anything against the training of cadets, but I take the risk of saying that the training of cadets in this country Is ot a military character, the idea behind it being to bring up a class of men who will have a relish for, and afterwards enter, the militia service. I do not think that it is desirable at the present time, in view of our financial condition, that we should spend money on anything which we can do without. The question is, can we do without the training of cadets just now? Can we do without the militia itself for a few years until we get over the crest of the hill?
Mr. LE.GER: Certainly.

Are we in a position
to spend money to-day for services of this kind? It was said yesterday that cadets were necessary in order to furnish men for the militia. Perhaps so. But I appeal for support in my contention that the present time is inopportune for us to spend money for this purpose. I appeal not only to the minister but to the hon. member for Victoria (Sir Sam Hughes), who perhaps has more experience and knowledge of military matters than any other man in Canada. I am not by any possible means1 saying that I always agree with the hon. gentleman; but if I were asked the question, who is the man in Canada that has the longest experience and the biggest soldier heart, who is the man that has given the most of his life to military training in this country-I would certainly say the hon. member for Victoria. I therefore appeal to him. When the militia of this country were obliged to go into the open in the Fenian Raid days of 1866, I think, or 1870, I venture to say that we had a class of stalwarts in the militia at that time that cannot be produced to-day. Again, at the time of the trouble in the West in 1885, I appeal to my hon. friend to endorse the opinion that a class of men jumped to arms in this country, as able and capable as could be found in any part of the world either then or to-day. I mention these two epochs in our history because, before 1866 and 1870 and for many 235	\
years afterwards, we had no cadet corps in this country. Up to 1885 we had no such corps in Canada, and I venture to think that there was not a single man of full age and fully developed physique in the last army that we raised who could in any way ascribe his physical ability and his courage to cadet corps training. I am speaking of my own part of the country, where there can be found men as strong and sturdy and brave as there are anywhere in the world. The men from that part of the country went to the front and won glory for themselves, and there i? no such thing in my county as a cadet corps worth mentioning. There are a few organizations here and there, but we have no cadet corps worth talking about. I do not want to tailk aiboult myself tout When I was growing up there was no such thing aB a cadelt corps. Yet I can stand about .as much hardship as any one. I was about as hardy a Scotch boy as was to be found anywhere, developed entirely through the ordinary games 'and .sports to which young men are usually drawn. There was no petticoat business as 'there is with this organization that iis spoken of now. I think it is very largely a waste of time to have boys going around the country with drumsticks in their hands and (wasting energy that might he better developed. I know the risk I am taking and the probable ridicule with which my remarks will toe received but I dd say 'that, in 'the condition of the country to-day when Iwe have no money to extend our railways to the fishing villages .along 'the coast where people are dying for want of proper transportation- not dying in the full sense of 'the term but praying and pressing 'for such development; when our harbours, breakwaters, wharves and public works cannot toe repaired and are -allowed to fall into, decay because the Department of Public Works tell us they have no money; when .all these things 'are crying out for the necessary .money to keep 'them up and to develop them in such a way as to help trade in this country and to lower the high cost of living, we -are nolt justified in (spending in the neighbourhood olf $400,000 for play of this kind that can very well he done without. These things are excellent amusements land possibly have a tendency to develop the mind of the boy in a. better direction than would be the case if there were no such 'training but I submit to the minister, the Government and this committee that there are occasions when there are greater calls than the purpose for which this vote is asked, which calls should

Yes, and of Kitchener, because he trained the schools there too. The cadet corps has been one of the chief supports of the militia and particularly durihg the late war.
(^ Sir SAM HUGHES: I may say to my hon. friend from North Cape Breton and Victoria (Mr. McKenzie), who has done me the honour to mention my name, that in the old Normal school days in the province of Ontario, Dr. Sangster, who was the principal of the Normal school in Toronto took up the matter of cadet training and Colonel Goodwin and his son who were excellent swordsmen and good shots did splen-

did work as instructors. No Normal school teacher was allowed to teach who was not qualified to engage in the training Of cadet corps in the schools. I wish toi draw my hon. friend's attention to the fact that when I was in charge of the Department of Militia and Defence there was scarcely a teacher in the province of Nova Scotia who was not fully qualified to teach the cadet corps and who had not a cadet corps certificate. I am sure that the splendid fellows who were, sent out from the schools oif North Cape Breton were inspired by the splendid work of the cadet corps in Nova Scotia. Nova Scotia took the matter up very actively through their public education department, under Dr. McKay I think. it was, and went into it very enthusiastically. I think the records showed that about 20,000 school teachers in the Dominion of Canada were qualified to instruct students in military drill, calisthenic exercises and physical training. The public at large, the churches and ladies' organizations were at one time opposed to this cadet movement believing that those who engaged in it had murder in their hearts. But those days have gone by and they now recognize its value. This principle is recognized:-
Beware the soft breathing that preaches of peace
With a pledge giving lip and a tear lighted eye.
Hear it all with good will but be provident still
With men that are earnest and powder that's dry.
That is good old North Cape Breton Presbyterian doctrine. I am glad that my hon. friend (Mr. McKenzie) grew up to be one of the most muscular chaps in the neighbourhood always ready to defend himself with his fists as well as with his tongue.

The hon. member for North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) has gone to the very heart of the matter in discussing the conditions which prevailed in Canada prior to the Fenian Raid and the Rebellion of 1885 in stating that the men of Canada in those days required no particular physical preparation for entering upon any military work. That is the fact due to the social and economic conditions which prevailed in those days. Because the social and economic conditions in Canada have gradually changed, and have brought about a new condition of life, it is necessary that we should have these cadet organizations to, in large measure, take the place of those very social and economic conditions which have changed through the

passing of time. In the old days the life which the people lived m'ore or less fitted them for military duties. The life which people live nowadays has an opposite or different effect. For that reason the cadet corps serve a tremendously useful purpose, as has been pointed out by the minister.
Although-1 have no Scotch blood in me I would like to protest against the observations of the hon. gentleman from Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) in referring to a certain form of military uniform as a petticoat business. I would like to point out that it may look like a petticoat but it is not.
I would fain disagree with the hon. member for North Cape Breton about his own tough looking appearance which he seems to pride himself on.
What was that last observation?
We would like to hear that observation.
The hon. member for North Cape Breton said he was about as tough a specimen as there was anywhere.
Physically.

Well, I do not say what. Otherwise, however, I do not agree with him. I think that the appropriation for the cadets should be in the Estimates of the Health Department. I have heard very many doctors say that there was absolutely nothing so good for the young men and the young women of that age as cadet training. It counteracts the student stoop; it tends to keep them straight, and prepares them for domestic life in accustoming themselves to the word of command. All these things are valuable and make for peace.
Not always.

It is not necessary to steer the young into military life simply because you endeavour to promote amongst them a sort of esprit de corps, of snappiness, a pride in their appearance, and of some sense of aversion'towards that sloppiness which is apt to characterize young people, when they reach a certain age if it is not counteracted. But the strongest argument for all this, as I say, is the doctors' argument. I am sure the member for Fort William (Mr. Manion) will agree with me when I say that the medical profession actually insist upon a continuance of cadet training for the purposes to which I refer. It should not, however, be confined to young men. Young women should have 2.35J
some of it and in the past they have had some of it. I have seen many exhibitions in which young women have formed themselves into companies have been properly trained, and afforded a great deal of entertainment to themselves and other people- useful entertainment. I do not think that such things as these which go to the. life, and to the bone and sinew, of the country should 'be treated lightly or as a matter of mere expense. They should be treated as a matter of health for whatever Government is in power we must have good men and wumen; aii-1 since nowadays the churches themselves confess that they are all gone to the dogs the least we -can do is to keep up the school and try to help them out.

I trust that the member who has just resumed his seat is speaking for his own church and not for the Presbyterian Church of Canada. I -will detain the committee for but a very short time this afternoon in offering some observations on this question of cadet services. I am quite willing that money should be spent on developing the health of the youth of Canada. I also agree most heartily with -the member for Peterborough (Mr. Burnham) that the young women and girls of Canada have just as great a claim upon the Government for help in the development of their physical powers as have the youth or the boys of Canada. I would like to say that if money is spent along these lines it should be given to organizations such as the Boy Scouts and the Girl Scouts rather than for Cadet Services. It does seem to me, Mr. Chairman, that those of the militarist frame of mind harve totally failed 'to learn the lessons of the recent Great War. We have listened last night in this House to speeches of a profoundly distressing and depressing character. We have heard men, whose reputations and whose characters we hold in high esteem, make statements which, if they mean anything mean this: That the war has 5 p.m. been fought in vain; that vre are just as far from a reasonable method of settling international disputes as we were in the year 1914; that there is just as much need for military and naval preparation; and that the reign of the Prince of Peace is just as far distant as it ever was. Sixty thousand of the bravest and best of Canadian youth-aye, not only of the youth but of even middle-aged and more matured manhood-lie under the sod of France and Flanders, yet the minister is asking us all the time to go back to the

scale of military expenditure which was in operation before 1914, I ask him, and I ask his supporters, if those boys died in vain? Is it as necessary now as it was then to spend the same amount of money and to give the same, and even more, time and thought to preparation for war?
What do you think about it yourself?

I think that this war
has proved that militarism is the most stupendous and gigantic failure that one can imagine.
Hear, hear.

I say that those men who come before their respective nations- just as the Minister of Militia came before us last night-and prate that the dignity and the honour of their country-the dignity and the honour of their country forsooth !-can only be supported by training men to kill each other-

Does the hon. member think that the men who did fight would have been less effective if they had been trained a little before the war broke out instead of, as it was, taking up so much time in training them?
I think it was proved in the last great war that those men who went into the army from civil life were, on the whole, more successful commanders, than the professional soldiers.
Hear, hear.

As one general-
'Sir SAM HUGHES: May I ask-

I would like to have
a chance to finish my point. As one general expressed it, they had less to unlearn than others who had been in military life before. I read with pride in a great English newspaper the other day that there were three outstanding corps commanders^ in the British army: One was the professional soldier, General Haldane; the other two were non-professional soldiers, one being from the Dominion of Australia, I Ithink General Monash, and the other our own Sir Arthur Currie. The two latter were civilians and when the war came they proved themselves to be splendid soldiers. Let me say this again-
Were not these so-called civilian generals tiained in the militia of Itheir respective countries, and for many years?

I knew nothing at all about General Monash, but I am aware that General Currie was a volunteer soldier of distinction.
Mr. STEiVENS:	Certainly, and he had
received a training such as we are trying (to make provision for now.
Mr. GRIEiSBACH: So was Monash.
Mr. McMiASTER:	Oh, I am surprised
that any militarist dares to face his fellow-beings. You have called for preparation; you have said: "Give us money and we will ensure you against war." Hon. members opposite smile; they think it is amusing. Well, is it amusing when a man feels these things in his heart and wishes in all sincerity to speak forth his inmost thoughts? You claimed that it was necessary to have preparation; you said that it would ensure the safety of the world if you only had a few armies and a few navies. And what has been the result? The result has been that a generation of young men in Europe has been wiped out. I heard the other day that a generation of young men in France who came to the age of about twenty in 1914 has practically been wiped out, and very much the same thing-
Mr. GRIESiBACfH: By what method might the French nation have avoided the war which fell upon them?
Mr. McMAlSTER: I have on a previous occasion said most emphatically that when one great nation set the pace it is very difficult indeed for other nations not to keep step. But I have also said this, and I repeat it : If one-tenth of the energy, the money and the thought that were devoted to arming one part of Europe against another had been devoted instead to bringing the different parts of Europe together, the war would not have come on.

Why did you not tell
them that before the war?

Just as in this House sneers and jibes are thrown at those who believe that there is a possibility of bringing mankind together, then as now there were those who sneered at efforts made to bring mankind together. There were great interests whose business it was to keep	the	various	nations on theverge of	w'ar in	order that they
might sell to them the instruments of destruction. There were English shareholders in Krupp's; there were German shareholders in the Armstrong-Whitworth firm and other concerns of that sort. There was an international trust for the purpose

of arming the different nations one against the other. Before the war the great nation of iGermany had apparently made up its mind that its destiny was to be either world-empire or downfall. They threw down the gauge of battle and it was not world-empire for them, thank God; it was downfall. But that frame of mind has received a check. That enemy is in the dust. Leaders in all the civilized nations of the world-not all leaders, I am sorry to say, but a great number of them- are endeavouring to form a League of rvavioixs. xl io \juhc ...nthat my hen. friend (Mr. Cockshutt) thought the League of Nations was a silly sort of thing. But after all it is a question of either a League of Nations or another war, unless nations are prepared to combine in order to develop some other reasonable and efficacious mode of settling international disputes. I am quite willing to admit that the present League requires serious change and serious modification. But there is one ideal laid before humanity-to try to organize a new world on a better basis. Then there is the other idea, the idea tO' get back to the prewar scale of military expenditure.
Last winter I had the honour of being at a dinner given for the young men of the church I go to who had been through the war. Some one hundred and thirty of them went out of the congregation, and some sixteen will never come back. But for those who came back we gave a complimentary dinner, and what struck me more than anything else, Mr. Chairman, was that these returned soldiers were just boys. In the world it has been the statesmen, the diplomats, the large business interests, the mature men, who have been responsible for the policies leading to war, but it has been the boys of the different nations that have fought and won the wars-or lost them, as the case may be. Surely it is time for Canada to set the pace toward a more reasonable condition of world organization. Surely we can try it. We are particularly favoured in this country; we are in such a position that we can without danger to ourselves make the experiment. The idea of a .quarrel between our neighbours to the south and ourselves is simply unthinkable; no one with any responsibility would contemplate .such a condition for a moment. That being the case, why not set the pace towards disarmament?
I ask you this, Mr. Chairman:	Is :it a
wise thing to bring up the youth of this land to be soldiers? I am willing to say that drill may be beneficial to physical development. I am even prepared to go fur-
.aa,
t-her and to say that a reasonable amount of drill has certain educational value. I am willing to have the youth of the country drill, but for the present at least, until we see whether or not this League of Nations is going to be a success, let us not develop the military side of the young man's mind; let us rather teach him cooperation for other purposes. When the distinguished soldiers who are in this House led their men on the battlefields of Europe I think they found that the Canadian, who, perhaps, had never had a uniform on hefnrp he enlisted, was man for man superior to his foe in actual conflict. When they came to hand-in-hand engagement, which, I understand, happens very seldom-they certainly were man for man the equal if not- superior to the enemy.
Why?

Because, for one reason, they had grown up in a country where universal military service was not enforced; because of the initiative and strength of character which is found in those who dwell in a country where the free development of individual character is encouraged; because of characteristics found in those who are not brought up in the atmosphere of a conscript nation. That is one reason, and that is one reason why if we wish to train the youth of this country in physical culture we may, for the time at least, divorce that idea from the military viewpoint. I have no objection to the country spending a reasonable amount-but let it be as reasonable as possible-[DOT] in training the youth along the lines of the co-operation of mental and physical development-and when I say "youth" I mean the girls, too; the girls should have their summer camps as well as the boys. But, in the name of common sense and viewing the fact that the militarists . have so entirely failed to do what they said they would do for their respective nations when they were bleeding them white by taxation, let us endeavour to conduct these camps, for the time being at least, without the military atmosphere.

I had not intended to delay the House in connection with these items; but I confess to yon, Sir, that sitting in my place and trying to fulfil my duties by being present in this House, I get somewhat wearied with the Pharisaical lectures that we are constantly treated to by the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster). A moment ago my hon. friend, in violation of the rules of the House addressing us directly, Sir, and ignoring the Chair, used the sweeping term "you militarists." I protest against

this; but I wish to draw the attention of the committee briefly to one of the preposterous arguments that he presented. He cited certain generals who had achieved a very high record at the front and he pointed to two who, he said, were civilians. Let me refer to the .Canadian one with whom we are all *acquainted. Sir Arthur Currie, during the early part of his life, in fact, right down to the breaking out of the war, had interested himself in military affairs under conditions exactly the same as those for which we are trying to make some provision at this time. Because of that training, because of that education, if you like, that he achieved, Sir Arthur Currie was fitted for the task which fell upon his shoulders later on. I can call to mind dozens of officers who when they went overseas, found that they were peculiarly fitted for the service that was laid upon their shoulders, but in every case they were men trained under the modified military training in our militia service. There is nothing militaristic about that; Canada has never had anything approaching a militaristic programme or system. My hon. friend says that we want to go back to prewar days and enter into this militaristic programme. We did not have a militaristic-programme in Canada in pre-war days. We certainly had not in the years 1911 to 1914, and my hon. friend will surely not charge his own friends with carrying out a militaristic programme from 1896 to 1911. Any man with any common sense knows perfect ly well that the militia expenditure of this country has been exceedingly modest from Confederation down.
My hon. friend says that it is quite desirable that some drill should be given; that it may have a good physical effect, and he is prepared to admit that it has an educative effect. But he .turns on us as soon as we propose just a moderate sum to provide for drill, and he charges us with trying to enforce militarism. Then he loads the whole responsibility of the commencement of this war upon those of us who have in mind a militia system in Canada.

May I rise to object
to that interpretation of my remarks? I loaded the responsibility on the diplomatists, the militarists and the large business interests.

My hon. friend included almost everybody except himself. He referred to us who were supporting the minister and to the minister's proposals. He likened the minister to the European militarists; he classed the minister and them

in the same group, and -then, of course, he went on to suggest that it was the militarists of Europe who brought on the war. But he failed to acknowledge this, that had poor France, faced with this huge military autocracy of Germany, not had a very severe system of conscriptive military service, she would not have been able to keep the Germans out of Paris for a week after the declaration of war. Under a militia system such as we have in this country, France would have been an easy simple victim to the military spirit and aggresion of Germany. We are not responsible for Germany, Russia, Austria, nor any of those other countries, but we are responsible for Canada.
My hon. friend says:	Let us wait until
we see whether the League of Nations is going to be a success. He made no argument; he gave no reasons; he simply offered some sweeping generalities. Supposing the League of Nations is not a success, we must, arguing from what he suggests, have a military force, because that was the suggestion in his remarks although it was not definitely stated. That is not the question at all. If the League of Nations is a success, each member of that League is going to be called upon to contribute at least something towards maintaining the dignity, power and control of that League. That provision is contained in the Treaties which have been laid before the various countries for ratification, and, therefore, we must have some moderate form of military power. All that we are asking for in these Estimates is that provision shall be made for-what shall I call it? It appeals to me as a skeleton army where some of our-men may give a great deal of their time willingly and without pay and may be brought together year after year for training.
The particular item under discussion is cadet corps. I know of no better discipline, education and training for young boys of .from twelve to fourteen or fifteen years of age than the cadet system of Canada. Not only is it physically sound and good, but there is this value to it. Young boys of that age, growing up from small boyhood and beginning to realize that they are budding into manhood, are mentally in a state where they easily drift and go astray. Every man who has had anything to do with boys or who has not forgotten his boyhood knows that. There is nothing better for a boy than to be held, not under forced restraint, but under restraint to which he willingly submits, and the cadet system supplies in

a most admirable manner this training and education.
But in the closing remarks of iny hon. friend, who, I notice, has now left his seat, he made a most extraordinary argument. His argument, in favour of no military training at all was that men from a country in which there is no military training at all have stronger combative forces.
More initiative.

-and more initiative than those who are trained in a country where military discipline obtains. - That is the very thing he was denouncing a moment before. He was denouncing the pugnacious spirit, the combative spirit; yet he would not have training because in that way the combative spirit develops. Why, in the name of common sense, should we be asked to put up, not only with my hon. friend's lectures, but with such piffling argument as that?
What I desire to say in rising in support of this item is, not that we should embark upon any great programme of militarism, but that we should retain in Canada, a reasonable, skeleton military force under the voluntary militia system; that we should not engage in nor embark upon wide expenditures in that line, but that reasonably generous support should be given to those citizens who devote after all to the militia about 75 per cent of 'their time, free of all charge to the country. Surely the country can at least pay the actual out-of-pocket expenses these men incur in connection with military training, and that is virtually all that we are being asked to do in this Estimate. I grant that there may be some points upon which hon. gentlemen opposite may reasonably differ from us, and these are fair matters for debate, but I resent the sweeping charge of my hon. friend that .simply because we stand behind these Estimates we belong to that obnoxious class known as European militarists.

limited to sharp shooting and specializing in machine gun practice and -work of that kind. My hon. friend from Brome may be surprised to	know that the	girlsin the schools of our province are trained in	calisthenics	and
physical exercises and military drill just the same as the boys in the public schools, as is well known to the great majority of the members of this House. I regret exceedingly to find my good friend the member for Brome delivering the same sort of stuff that was handed out to the people of Canada before the war by the Rev. Dr. Starr Jordan and Ithe Rev. J. A. Macdonald.

It was not my intention to say anything in this debate, but I resent some of the remarks thalt have been made on the other side of the House. I do not think it is fair to represent members on this side of the House as militarists, and it is not fair or Itrue to say that we have not learned the lessons of this war. For two days now we have been listening to a repetition, almost word for word, of the speeches that were delivered in this House on military matters in the years previous to 1914, and if there is one class of speech thalt hon. mem'beTS on the other side of the House ought to be willing to forget, surely it is that class. History has shown that hon. gentlemen opposite were totally incapable of appreciating the significance of the events of their time. There is not a man living to-day with a son of public school age who would not disown his boy if after the experience of the last five years he put the same construction on these matters as hon. gentlemen opposite do to-day. They tell us we have not learned the lessons of the war. Certainly we are not going to sit at their feet to learn the lessons of Ithe last four or five years, and when they tell us here this afternoon that we are incapable of learning from the experience of the last four or five years, I say they are talking about things of which they are incapable of giving an opinion of any value. Who in Canada to-day believes that if England had been prepared for the war in 1914, as she should have been prepared, the war would ever have taken place? It is the opinion of a great many leading military men in England and in France that even if England in the days just before the war had taken a more decided step and answered in the affirmative the telegram sent by the President of France to King George, the great

war would have never been started. It is absurd to say in the face of a modest sum like this that we are starting this country on a military career. The leader of the Opposition yesterday objected very strenuously and worked himself up into a pitch of passion against these military Estimates, and in those Estimates he included the money we are granting for pensions to widows and orphans.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I took no exception whatever to such expenditures. My objection was taken exclusively to the items that appear in these Militia and Defence Estimates.

I submit
that he included them in the total which he quoted to the House, and included also the sums to be voted for the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment.

speechtext: I took no exception to those items.

He says
now that he took no exception to them. I say that he figured up a total of $50,000,000 or $60,000,000. I want to tell him that this country is prepared to go even further in the matter of pensions for widows and orphans and for the disabled soldiers. He also objected very strenuously to certain sums provided in these Estimates for training, and said "We have an army of trained men." Yes, we have, and that army saved the honour of Canada in the last five years. And it ill becomes any member in this House to stand up and berate them for the paltry sum of money that is put into these Estimates for carrying on the work of the department. Hon. gentlemen tell us that we have an army of trained men and we do not need any more training. I ask the leader of the Opposition this question: Does he think that the work of these men is never done? I say, Mr. Chairman, that their work is completed so far as this generation is concerned, and it lies with this House and this country to make provision for training osiers in case of necessity. ,It is all very well to talk about cutting down Estimates, but I notice that when there was trouble in Winnipeg a year ago it was the soldiers to whom this Government and the country turned. So soon as the hour of danger is passed, however, then there is nothing but a strong advocacy of retrenchment, and a decrying of everything that appertains to the training of. our youth. Hon. gentlemen decry the proposal to give these boys even a couple of weeks training in the

summertime; and they are opposed to putting up decent barracks for the men to live in and giving to the officers the necessary money [DOT]which they have to spend in order to keep up their regiments. They want to give only a portion of that money. I would ask the 'House to get down to actual facts. Is there a man here rwho is willing to go out and do the work that these men are doing for the same money? If there is then let him undertake the task. I say it is not becoming to any member of this House to sit here and ask the men who saved the

were staying at home, to be prepared to save it again in the future. It ill behooves any member to say that we should make no provision for the training of new men but should let those who have carried the burden for the last five years carry it in the future. That, Mr. Chairman, is not the spirit that should quicken hon. members. To my mind, the House should approach this question with different feelings. I, as much as any one else, would deprecate the establishment of a military party in Canada; but the man, the party, or the country that does not to-day make at least some provision for self-defence has not, in my humble opinion, learned the lessons from the experience of the last four or five years.

Mr. Chairman, I desire to detain the House just a moment. First of all, I should like to say a word with regard to what was said by the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria (Mr. McKenzie) concerning the advantages of cadet training, and the inference, from his remarks, that the trained cadets in this country did not show up as well in the late war as those who were not trained. I want to refer to one school I know something of where the boys were trained as cadets. Of those boys that had training, one hundred per cent of the physically fit enlisted fox overseas service and made up a portion otf that 44,000 to whom the Minister of Militia has referred; and a very large number of them, I regret to say, will not come back. On the side of advantage generally which the cadet training has, I would say without hesitation that there is nothing that is better for any boy's physical development and future manhood than such training. There is nothing that so much tends to make a true man of a boy as the training he gets as a cadet when going to school; and if this country could aim at having every boy trained as a cadet it would go a long way towards developing
the right type of Canadian man. There is no question that the Canadian soldier, whether trained or untrained, was a good soldier; but to infer that the man wh'o had training was less of a soldier than the man who had not, is to fly in the very face of what every one knows to be an absolute fact. Turning to what has been said by my hon. friend from Brome (Mr. McMaster) and what was repeated this afternoon and yesterday so frequently in regard to the whole question of the militia of Canada, the charge has been hurled across the House that these membQrG ciiTvnorting the Minister of Militia are militarists. It has been suggested that we are following in the footsteps of the German junkers, and all that sort of thing, and that we have failed to appreciate the fact that ias a result of militarism 60,000 of the best of Canada's sons are sleeping in France. Well, Sir, I resent that imputation. We do not fail, nor have we ever failed, to appreciate the fact that
60,000	of Canada's sons are now at rest in France. We fully realize the fact; and if Canada and England had not listened to the snivelling pacificists in the days before the war, there would have been fewer Canadian sons sleeping in France to-day than there actually are. It was the very fact that the counsel of such men as the late Lord Roberts was wholly ignored, and the fact that the British Empire was in a state of unpreparednees, that brought on that awful international condition that ultimately resulted in universal disaster. Had the British Empire, at the outbreak of the war, had one-eighth of the trained men which it was finally necessary that she should place on the field, they would have ended the war in less than one year, the national debt about which we hear .so much would have been very much smaller than it is, and many of the boys who ultimately gave their lives for our sake would have been spared to us. Just one wiord further, Mr. Chairman. It has been said that Canada is a law-abiding country and that there is no possibility of war with our neighbours to the south. Well, it is true that Canada is a law-abiding country, and it is equally true that we are living beside a nation that is law-abiding. But if we are going to carry our law-abiding precepts to the point suggested by hon. gentlemen opposite, why do we not propose that every town and city and village in Canada should disband its police force? The people in the city of Ottawa are law-abiding. Nevertheless, we see many uniformed men patrolling the streets

all the time. The people in the -United States are also law-abiding; yet there is a national guard in every State ol the Union. Why is that? The reason is simple. Tfaerfj is in every country under the sun a certain element that would break the law, and it is the duty of the State to see to it that law-abiding people are protected; and they can be protected only by having some sort of organized force for the purpose. Will hon. gentlemen opposite seriously contend that by passing these Estimates we shall develop militarism in this country? If they do they insult the intelligence not only of this House but of the people of the country, and they are implying something which gentlemen on this side of the House have every right to resent. Personally I strongly resent the implication that because we are supporting the Minister of Militia in regard to these Estimates we advocate militarism, develop German junkerism and-the greatest insult of all-fail to appreciate the great sacrifice made by our boys in the late war. A more contemptible suggestion could not be offered to dozens of men who are sitting in this House, and for my own part I repeat -again that I -resent the insult with all the force which I can put into my words and with all the feeling I have in my being.

Mr. 'Chairman, you are absolutely right in your ruling. However, I was just about through with that line of argument when you very properly brought me to task. In regard to this cadet service I want to say that while I believe there may be some very strong differences of opinion in regard to holding the annual militia drill in this country at the present time, I just as sincerely believe that you have the majority of public opinion behind the cadet service; that from one end of this country to the other people are behind that particular service.
