Militia and Defence-contingencies, $50,000.
How does the amount of this item compare with the similar item in pre-war years?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: , Last year the amount voted was $25,000; in 1918-19 it was $5,337. The normal amount used for the purpose in pre-war years was $50,000. It covers all such items as telephone messages, telegrams, legal expenses, allowances to officiating clergymen at permanent force stations, medals, guards of honour, escorts, salutes, State and military funerals, and all unforeseen expenses not provided for elsewhere.
If we could get along last year with $25,000 what is our difficulty in getting along with the amount this year?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Last year a good many of these expenditures were probably charged to demobilization. A great many of them were directly connected with the war, or were so treated during the war period. So with all classes of militia expenditure. Wherever barracks were used for Canadian Expeditionary troops, all repairs and things of that kind were charged to War Appropriation, not to the annual Militia vote. This vote is to cover all unforseen miscellaneous expenditure.
Could the hon. gentleman give a rough subdivision of these items?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
No, I have no subdivision of them. The amount is lumped

in the way I have given it. I think that is about as nearly as we can estimate it. It is irregular, unforeseen expenditure; it is in its nature contingent.

When I said "subdivision" I meant "classification." For instance, it might be interesting to know how much we invested in allowances to officiating clergymen during a given year. Then there are -the items: "legal expenses," "guards of honour", "escorts", "salutes"; could my hon. friend tell us roughly what sum will be required for each of these branches of the service? With regard to the item of "legal expenses", for example, there is the fact to be considered that -we have our Department of Justice; that each branch of the Government has its legal advisor. I take it for granted that there must be some good reason for this part of the item, but one is naturally curious to know what legal expenses are contemplated.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Legal expenses are incurred at times by various departments at outside points. During my brief experience in this department I have on several occasions had to employ counsel in various parts of Canada to represent the Department of Militia. We can very often get a local man for $5 or $10, whereas the cost of sending a man from Ottawa would be very much greater. Hardly a day passes without there being some legal questions to settle in some part of Canada in connection with which we employ some local legal practitioner. As to the officiating clergymen at permanent force stations, there are Protestant and Roman Catholic clergymen in attendance and the basis upon which they are paid is at the rate of fifty cents per man per year.
I do not question the propriety of paying clergymen; the department needs the benefit of their services, and I would not like to deprive them of that benefit.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
During the
afternoon some hon. members opposite seemed to express the view that we of the Opposition were not wholly in sympathy with even legitimate expenditure for the militia at this time. I think it is only proper to point out that the criticism that we have made of the Militia Estimates relates to the amounts that are brought in at this particular time. Our criticism has not been directed against the making of reasonable expenditures for proper militia purposes; it has been wholly against the expenditures of large sums of money on

this account while we have appropriations in the Estimates for the purposes of demobilization also. When the work of demobilization is completed, we may well consider grounds for incurring further expenditures, meanwhile expenditures cep* tainly should not be charged to demobilization where appropriations are voted for specific purposes. As every one knows, the reasons that have existed in the past for apprehending danger from a military point of view do not now exist; there is not the same need for alarm in the matter of our defence at home. We on this side nffo-r rv? opposition to legitimate expenditures for the needs of the country, but where it is evident that the expenditures are extravagant we feel justified in asking the Government, at a time when they are putting extra taxes on the people to cut down suoh expenditures. Now, this is an item of $50,000 to cover miscellaneous and unforeseen expenses, allowances to officiating clergymen at permanent force stations, legal expenses, guards of honour, escorts, salutes, and so on. There is nothing in that whole programme that is vital; the country would not suffer one iota if for a year we abolished salutes altogether or got rid of some of the escorts, and extras of that kind in respect of which we can well afford to economize. These things constitute the fuss and feathers and the display which are more or less unessential. The amount asked is $25,000 in excess of what was asked last year. Unless the minister can show more conclusively the necessity for increasing the amount to $50,000, I will move that the amount of the Estimate be reduced from $50,000 to $25,000-an amount quite sufficient for the miscellaneous purposes cited here.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I am sorry that I cannot give the details my hon. friend (Mr. Fielding) requested, but I can give some information with regard to the various matters. Of course this is only an estimate; if we do not have the money we have no way of paying for the service. Legal expenses which crop up are all in the nature of unforeseen expenses. I do not know when they may come up. It may be that for a year there will be no legal expenses, though that is unlikely. As the committee is well aware, guards of honour are furnished to His Excellency the Governor General and to the Lieutenant Governors of the various provinces of Canada. A guard of honour costs in the neighbourhood of $100 to $125. An escort is a little more expensive; it costs probably about $200, and it is
furnished to the Governor General only. On a military funeral a limit of expense of about $65 or $70 is set. State funerals are very rare, and when they occur, they involve a large amount of money.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Does the minister contemplate any State funerals?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: We do not know when they will happen. The last one occurred quite recently. It is one of the things that we desire to provide for; it is a contingency, and the money, if not required, is not wasted it merely remains in the ap'propria-tion. It is quite possible that $25,000 might suffice; it is quite likely that $25,000 might not suffice. No waste is involved in this item; all the expenditure must go before the Auditor General. The legal expenditure, as such, must go to the Department of Justice and be certified there before it is paid. Therefore, my hon. friend's amendment does not involve one feature of saving. The appropriation is just as secure in its present form-and it is just an estimate -as it would be if the amendment carried. I do not see any object or reason for my hon. friend's amendment. If he objects to guards of honour or escorts and says that they should be dispensed with, he should say so; but on a contingent item on which one can make only a guess, to say that his guess is nearer than my guess is rather ridiculous. In pre-war times $50,000 was the usual amount appropriated, and it was not always spent. The year immediately preceding the war we spent $51,000; last year the appropriation was $25,000, but I am not sure what was spent. As far as we can estimate, $50,000 is a safe sum to put into the Estimates, and what expenditure takes place will be scrutinized by the Government and the officials of the Government, and the vote will be carefully administered. I do not see what the object of the amendment of the leader of the Opposition really is, unless it be a demonstration of some kind,-there is no principle involved in it. What should be stricken out? What should we dispense with? If the hon. member will express himself and let the committee know what he objects to in the proposal, we shall then know how to deal with the matter.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
If my hon.
friend's reasoning amounts to anything, I do not see why he should not have made the item $100,000 instead of $50,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
We considered $50,000
would be sufficient.,

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The purpose
of an .appropriation is to put some restriction on a department in the matter of designated expenditures. I take direct exception to haying for this particular year so many guards of honour and salutes and to paying clergymen for officiating at functions of the permanent force as outlined in tire details of this Estimate. When we come to a different time it may perhaps be well to have some of these decorations, but decorations I think they are. Laslt year, His Excellency had such guards of honour as he needed. I do not think the country lacked guards of honour or salutes, and if $25,000 was sufficient for last year, it is enough for this year, and anything over that is just a waste of public funds.

speechtext:

the stationery item is a correct item. It covers the supply of stationery to all the units of the Canadian Expeditionary Force.

That
does not alter the fadt that the total amount of contingencies during the past year, the year represented in the Auditor General's Report, was only about $17,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
This covers customs
dues which we have on our imports, and it is really a matter of bookkeeping, taking the amount out of the Militia Department and handing it over to the Customs Department. Prior to Ithe -war the appropriation for this service was generally from $100,000 to $125,000. I think I am correct in saying that the department has been employing customs brokers for making entries at the ports where these goods come in. I am surprised to find charges of that kind in the Auditor General's report. We have a War Purchasing Commission, and a purchasing agent, I believe, in the Department of Militia. We have .also customs officers. With this galaxy of Government officers I do not think it ought to be necessary to employ the services of customs brokers to make the entries. Will the minister explain why these customs brokers are employed?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
All our purchases are made by the W.ar Purchasing Commission; the department merely makes the requisition. I am informed that only at one point Is a customs broker employed, and that is at the port of Quebec where the majority of our purchases are entered for the Dominion arsenal there. We have been in the habit of employing a customs broker there who receives the magnificent sum of $1 per entry. It is considered more economical to employ him than to have the work done

by our own officers. If we did it ourselves it would entail the employment probably of an extra clerk. We are simply doing what many business men do; it is looked upon as good business to employ a customs broker at the port where our chief business is done.
Dominion Arsenal, Lindsay, $258,112.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: How does the minister justify this expenditure at * this time?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: For a number of years *nqct. n11 >* reserve supply of ammunition has been based upon a report which was made to the Government of Canada by Lord French after he had made a complete survey of our 'whole military situation. In his report he recommended that we should maintain a reserve supply of 90,000,000 rounds of small arm ammunition.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: When was that report made?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
In 1910, before the
change of Government. We have endeavoured ot maintain that as a reserve, but during the war that standard was not maintained. I do not, suppose I .am making known any secret that I should not miake known when I say that to-day we have on hand between 35,000,000 and 40,000,000 rounds. The annual output has heretofore been estimated at 10,00,000 rounds. This year there is provision in the Estimates for .an output of 11,500,000 rounds. If our militia establishment was complete-it is not so, as I explained yesterday-it would utilize from 7,000,000 to 8,000,000 rounds, exclusive of what we supply to Dominion and provincial rifle associations. The annual supply to these associations, which are established by law .and by practice in this country, is from 1,500,000 to 2,000,000 rounds. Allowing between 7,000,000 and 8,000,000 rounds for the militia to be used in practice and drill, we would have a surplus each year of about 3,000,000 rounds. That, of course, would be added to our reserve stock, which it is our ultimate aim to bring up to the standard recommended by Lord French, but it will take some time to do it. We thought that if we entered upon a programme this year of 11,500,000 rounds, 5,500,000 to be made at Lindsay and 6,000,000 at Quebec, that was about all we could ask the House to consider at this time. We really should have a larger supply if we are to bring up our reserve within a reasonable time. However, as
this year may be a slack year in the expenditure of small arms ammunition, it is possible that our reserve may make a considerable gain. The item for the Lindsay arsenal represents what we believe will be the actual cost of manufacture. We have at Lindsay, Ontario, one of the best-equipped factories I suppose that can be found anywhere for the manufacture of this ammunition. The items which go to make up this cost are as follows: Wages, $153,000-we pay the union wage scale, upon schedules furnished by the Department of Labour-salaries for the officers in connection with the arsenal, $13,000; power and light, $10,000; water, $2,400; steam coal, $18,900; pea coal, $6,500; supplies, $50,312; fi eight, $3,000; office supplies, telephones, etc., $1,000; total, $258,112.
Is the power for the Lindsay arsenal supplied by the Hydro-Electric?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Either that or a private company, but I think it is the Hydro.
Hoiw much is paid for power?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: If it is the Hydro.it will be the ordinary provincial rate. The rate is much higher in Ontario than in that part of the province of Quebec from which my hon. friend comes.
Who is now the director of the Lindsay .arsenal? I understand that the late Coibneil Laffetty was director. Who replaced h'iffi on his death?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Colonel Lafferty was director at Quebec.
Was he not direictor at Lindsay also?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: During the war he was appointed superintendent, for a time, of both arsenals. A:t present the superintendent at Lindsay is Mr. Walters. I do not know his military rank, or whether he has any. He is spoken of as Professor Walters.
How many men are employed at Lindsay a(t present?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I have not the exact figures, but I am informed about 230 men.

Is it not a fact that the Quebec arsenal was quite 'Sufficient for our needs, except for a certain period during the war when 'munitions were urgently needed on the other side? In normal times would not the Quebec arsenal be 'amply sufficient .for the needs of our militia?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: As between the tiwo arsenals I think Lindsay would be the better adapted, bult there are military reasons foT maintaining Ibbth arsenals. I believe the cbmstrudtion of the two .arsenals was advised by >a high military authority, for reasons whiteh are obvious. I believe that either one has the capacity to turn out a sufficient ontput in peace times. Neither of them i!s being operated to its capacity at the present time.
How many men are there at the Queibec airsenial?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: At the present time neajrly 500. All Puir heavy ammunition and quick-firing ammunition, as well as a large part of our rifle ammunition, is made at Quebec. Lindi&ay only manufactures at present fem.aH arms ammunition; I do not think it has the equipment for making artillery ammunition.
I am informed that the munitions turned out by 'the Quebec arsenal were highly commended by military authorities during the war. Is that a fact?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I understand that our ammunition has been very highly commended, both that made at Quebec and that made at Lindsay. I doubt if any better ammunition is turned out anywhere.

Are they making at
Lindsay a little device known as a steel charge or clip used by the soldier for holding a set of five cartridges for the certain and speedy filling of the magazine of the rifle in action ?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
If I understand my hon. friend's question, he wants to know whether we are making steel charges.
Mr.	MORPHY:	At	Lindsay.Mr.	GUTHRIE:	I	understand	that	we
are making them at Lindsay.

At Quebec also?
Mr.	GUTHRIE:	Yes.

What is the price per
pound of the steel that is being used?
Mr.	GUTHRIE:	I	have not	got	these
particulars; I would have to communicate with Lindsay.

I should like to know
also what number of these clips are bing made this year.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I understand that the
clips are being manufactured at the rate of one to five cartridges, so that if we make five million cartridges w-e shall make one million clips.
(Mr. I.e.'nieux.]

Uan I get the cost of
the manufacturing of these clips?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: The information could be obtained, but I would have to communicate with Lindsay.

My main reason for asking this question is that in the constituency I have the honour to represent a man who manufactured these charges during the war lost "something like $50,000 because, as he alleges, the War Purchasing Commission compelled him to use steel at 14 cents a pound although, he further alleges, steel at 7j cents per pound was being used by other manufacturers. I desire this information in order to see exactly what has been and is being done at Lindsay. I want to know the quality of steel used there, and the price. I might also commend to the minister the circumstances of this case and request him to investigate it. The names and particulars he can obtain, and I should be glad if he would see whether or not there is any way of recompensing this man who claims that he sustained this tremendous loss through no fault of his own but by reason of the arbitrary conduct of the Government inspectors who, he alleges, showed favoritism to other firms. He is firm in the statement that he was not responsible in any way for the loss, which he says was due to a rigid inspection that was discriminatory, and to other unwarrantable conduct on the part of the departmental officials, by reason of which he has been brought to bankruptcy and practically put out of business.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I cannot at the present moment give the particulars my hon. friend desires. My information is that this is the first time the matter has been brought to the attention of the department. It may have been brought before the War Purchasing Commission, but that would not necessarily bring it to the attention of the Militia Department. I can inform my hon. friend that the steel that is being used at Lindsay in the manufacture of these clips is purchased by the War Purchasing Commission itself and handed over to the Lindsay arsenal. I have no doubt I could secure the information by hon friend desires, and if he will write me a letter indicating the details which he would like to get I will undertake to obtain the information.

The minister can get all the details from the chairman of the War Purchasing Commission. All the fact* are

on file, but they say that they have no power to deal with the case at all.

There is an increase in
this item, over the pre-war vote, of almost $500,000. Can the minister give some explanation as to the cause of this increase?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I have no doubt that
increase is due to increased cost of material and increased wages. Wages have been raised from time to time in accordance with the prevailing rates, and at present they are fixed by the Department of Labour. There has been a tremendous increase in wages as also in the cost of material, and I am satisfied that the difference in cost between manufacturing now and in pre-war times is attributable entirely to these two factors, labour and material.

Does the minister think that it is wise to go ahead with the manufacture of this ammunition on a large scale under the present heavy increase in cost? Apparently there is no particular urgency for it in the next few years, and I would suggest that it might be worth while cutting down the output and thereby reducing the expenditure until we get 'back to normal costs.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I explained this as fully as I could a moment ago-I do not know whether my hon. friend was in the House at the time-and I do not think I can add anything to my statement. We are trying to make up our exhausted reserve. I suppose we might take chances, but I do not think it would be proper to do so. The Government is charged with responsibility in the matter, and I know that if we did not make up that reserve we would be properly 'blamable.

I am still not satisfied with the explanation the minister has given.
Mr. 'GUTHRIE: I cannot give any better.	[DOT]

I regret that. Nevertheless, every country is in the same position. I venture to say that all countries are exhausted after the war, and I think that the people will look with some apprehension upon this desire to continue our military expenditure in this respect on the basis that we maintained before the war.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: It has been stated during the course of the debate, both yesterday and to-day, that all countries are reducing their military expenditures.
We are increasing ours.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: We are increasing it at a less ratio than any other country that took part in the war. Think of the United States, with $645,000,000 this year, including $40,000,000 for Air Service. And there is an increase above ours in Australia,-I do not know about New Zealand, but I can' make that statement in regard to Australia. There is an increase in Great Britain. I have no information regarding France, but I understand that she is taking no chances. Our increase is a modest one. Japan is ccrtaimy mcicasixig eiiumiuusiy. And as a matter of fact ours is not increased at all having regard to pre-war prices; considering pre-war prices, there is a positive decrease. I have tried to impress this fact on the committee, but I believe that there are people who will object no matter how low the expenditure goes. However low it may be they will want it lower, but we have reached what we regard as a reasonable minimum.

My information, obtained through the War Purchasing Commission, in connection with the matter of which I spoke a moment ago, is that they have anywhere from twenty to thirty millions of these steel clips on hand. If that is so, there is no justification whatever-assuming that these clips are available to the Militia Department-for manufacturing a million more at Lindsay. The discussion shows me clearly that there is overlapping and lack of co-operation between the War Purchasing Commission and the Militia Department, and I think it is my duty to call the minister's attention to what appears to me to be a serious case of over-production of material, apart altogether from the principle of the increase in manufacturing. I would ask the minister to look into this matter. If he does he will probably find that I am right; and if I am not right I can tell him now that this over-production has been urged as a reason why they did not do the square thing by the gentleman whom they drove into bankruptcy.
My hon. friend stated a moment ago that the arsenal at Lindsay was the result of a visit of Lord French.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: No; I said the result of advice which the Government had received in regard to this question of establishing arsenals; I do not know that it was received from Lord French.

My hon. friend stated so positively, a moment ago.



Mr. 'GUTHRIE: No; we established the reserve of ammunition on his report.

I was in the Government when Lord French came to Canada. That was in 1910. I remember his visit very well. The Government that succeeded was rather inactive, as this arsenal was only started long after the war commenced. At the time, it struck several that it was something else than the report or advice of Lord French which institgated the building of the arsenal at Lindisay. Everybody at that time thought there was some rivalry between the gentleman who was at the head of the Militia Department and some other official, and naturally he thought his own constituency might have the advantage, if it is an advantage, of securing this large arsenal. I am informed-I am not much of a military man myself-that, under normal conditions and in normal times, Canada can well 'be satisfied with the arsenal at Quebec for all stores that will 'be required in Eastern or Central Canada. Why should we keep 250 men at Lindsay and 500 at Quebec during peace times? My hon. friend (Mr. Guthrie) will admit with me that it is too much. He should receive some inspiration to-day from his distinguished colleague the hon. member for St. Antoine (Sir Herbert Ames). That hon. gentleman comes here as the authorized representative of the League of Nations. Officially he occupies a seat in the Bureau of the League of Nations, and in day or so he will ask this Parliament to vote quite a large sum of money as being Canada's share of the cost of maintenance of the League of Nations. I, for my part, intend to support the hon. member for St. Antoine in that move, because I believe it iff a praiseworthy one. I stand for the League of Nations. But I do not stand for too much militaristic display. Really, my hon. friend does not seem to 'be in earnest when he asks from this committe sufficient to maintain the war equipment and the war display. Let us stand by the old arsenal at Quebec, which received so much commendation during the war from the Imperial authorities, and let us close the Lindsay arsenal.

speechtext:
The hon. gentleman

Mr. iBUREAU:	They must have done

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
It is remarked that it
is at a point farther removed from the frontier, less subject to outside attack, and more modern in equipment, than the arsenal at Quebec. I did not suggest that General French had said anything about the arsenal but I said that my information was that the Imperial authorities had suggested the propriety of having more than a single arsenal. The Minister of Militia at this time, the hon. member for Victoria (Sir Sam Hughes), in his wisdom located that arsenal at the city of Lindsay. I have no doubt it is a very excellent location for such an establishment. But in the meantime my view is that the two establishments can be carried on without any very great loss. I believe we could consolidate them; we could manufacture the whole of this ammunition at Lindsay or at Quebec. But there are military reasons for maintaining two establishments. A-s soon as we reach a normal surplus probably the output of both these institutions will be materially cut down; but we have not got that reserve on hand yet.

the 'War Appropriation. speechtext: Did the Minister of Militia, at the time, inform the *House that these expenditures were to be taken out of the demobilization vote?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
These two expenditures, one at Quebec and one at Lindsay, should be taken together. For the arsenal at Lindsay the Government are asking for an appropriation of $258,112, and for the arsenal at Quebec $532,512, both for the same purpose, the manufacturing of small-arms ammunition. That makes a total of $790,000 that the country is being asked to contribute for the manufacture of small-arms ammunition at this time. According to the Government's own statement the total expenditure for this purpose in the year before the war was $300,000.
In other words the Government is asking Parliament to-day to vote $490,000 more for the manufacture of small-arms ammunition than was asked from Parliament in the year preceding the war. That, Mr. Chairman, is an increase of expenditure that, to my mind, is not only unjustifiable but outrageous, and if the ministry will not listen to the suggestions that have been made we shall be obliged by a vote to record our opinion in favour of cutting that expenditure down. I therefore would move that this item be reduced by $150,000, and when we come to the vote for the Quebec arsenal I shall suggest a reduction in that expenditure of $250,000, thus endeavouring to save the country $400,000 on the manufacture of small-arms munition this year I 'think that if we asked to decrease this expenditure by even half a million that would not be demanding too much in the way of reduction. When the minister speaks of a report by Lord French on the necessity of keeping a reserve of ammunition, he knows very well that Lord French was one of those British officers who believed in the near approach of war and an 236J
impending menace, and that he was naturally anxious that the different countries of the Empire should have a substantial reserve of small-arms ammunition. But if Lord French came to this country to-day he would not make a report of that kind, as the minister well knows. The necessity for a reserve to-day and the necessity for a reserve before the war are two entirely different things. Besides, there is plenty of time to make good this reserve. The minister, I venture to say, does not contemplate any emergency requiring the use of small-arms ammunition within the next few years, and there must be a great quantity of this ammunition somewhere about at the present time as the result of supplies that were accumulated during the war. I therefore move that this item be reduced by $150,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
My hon. friend points
to the amount that was spent before the war and the amount that is spent now. I think that the estimate before the war was over ten million rounds, and the cost of it now is just about double what it was. I have given the reasons-the cost of material and the cost of labour have doubled. I do not share my hon. friend's views as to whether we should have a reserve or not. My own view, and that of the Government, is. that, we should maintain the reserve. I do not know where my hon. friend gets his knowledge of what Lord French would, do if he were here to-day. I know what he did when he was here and what report he made, and he came here at the instance of the Government of which my hon. friend was a member. I fancy that if he came here to-day he would, be just as sane in his view, and would recommend a substantial reserve notwithstanding the increased cost. I have just as much right to assume that, as my hon. friend has to make the rather foolish assumption he made.

sons. We are not engaged in battle at the present time; this is a time of peace; we are considering these matters in Parliament; and I think our common sense view of things is just as sane as is any recommendation that Lord French might make under the existing circumstances.
