When the war broke out, instead of using the drill hall that belonged to them the Government opened up this other place. It was only after the Rioux arsenal had been in use for two years or thereabouts that the Government, having been censured by the newspapers for this blunder, decided to use the other place. There is no use for two drill halls in Riviere du Loup.
May I aisk the hon. member for K a mourns k a (Mr. Stein) if this is the same Rioux who was suspended by the Bar Association of Quebec?

Yes.
Mr. MAR'CIL (Bonaventure): When the minister says that he is looking around Montreal for another site for barracks, do I understand him to mean that the Dorval property is to be abandoned? On whose advice was that property purchased and what was the pricer

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I do not desire my hon. friend to understand me to say that any definite conclusion has been reached in regard to the Dorval property. The question of disposing of it is under consideration; but unless we can dispose of it to advantage I do not for a moment say that action will be taken. Inquiries have been made in regard to other properties in the city of Montreal. I do not know at present what the property cost, from whom it was purchased, or when it was purchased. If my hon. friend desires that information I can undertake to get it for him to-morrow.
I am afraid the Government will not get what they paid for it.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
That is often the case
with private property.
Who looks after the drill hall at Levis?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I understand there is
a caretaker there but at the moment I cannot give his name.
What is his salary?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: When we come to the item of salaries and wages I can give all that information. His salary is $120 a year; his name is Richard.
When was he appointed?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I have not got that information now. I will try to get it when we come to the item of salaries and wages.
On whose recommendation was the appointment made?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I have no knowledge of that. If these questions are material, when we come to salaries and wages I shall be glad to furnish the necessary information.
Ordnance, Arms, Lands, etc., $10>0,0'00.

Would
local companies organized in battalions be given any money under the item in the details:	" Grants to Rifle Associations,
Active Militia Bands, Military Institutions and Regimental Associations"?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Local companies are
not entitled to grants.
What I mean is, are any grants given to local companies in the way of assisting them to organize and carry on?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
The only assistance
that is given is the grant made to the officer commanding. He is paid at the rate of 60 cents per man of the company.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Will the minister please explain this item?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
This item is to provide for transport of heavy ordnance and field guns; for the reserve of mobilization stores; ammunition, small arms, saddlery, harness and transport vehicles, also for the inspection, maintenance and repairs of same; for the cost of inspection of all ordnance; for the purchase of land for camp grounds, rifle ranges, drill halls, etc.; for all expenses and disbursements in connection therewith. Before the war, the annual expenditure under this vote was in the neighbourhood of $2,000,000. At the present time there is considerable reserve on hand of clothing and military stores. The ordnance used overseas is being returned rapidly to Canada, so that for the present and for some time to come I do not anticipate that it will be necessary for us to purchase any ordnance. The annual provision that must be made for the coming year will be the cost of inspection of am-

munition. There will be some changes, I believe, in the howitzer equipment, to conform to the British pattern. A few small purchases of land remain to be completed; I have not the details of those land purchases. It is estimated that the expenditures under this item will amount to $100,000. '

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The minister
said that this item was to cover expenditures for rifle ranges and drill halls. Might I remind him that he informed the House yesterday that the department had altogether some $3,500,000 or $4,000,000 worth of land that they did not know what to do with and that they were thinking of disposing of it and taking the proceeds to help to meet the expense of putting up barracks. Under these circumstances does the minister think he can justify asking for a further expenditure for rifle ranges and drill grounds?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: These are small portions of land that may be wanted here or there to extend a range or drill ground. It is only a contingent matter. I do not know what these pieces of land may be. There may be none at all. But the question of rifle ranges is a large one. To take the situation right here in Ottawa, I am informed that we have in the Connaught ranges perhaps the most highly equipped and best rifle range on the continent of America. The only difficulty is that it is five or six miles away from street car service. We are waiting for the extension of the car line, but there does not seem to be much of a prospect of that in the near future. We have a very valuable property at Rockcliffe. My information is that when the Connaught range was purchased it was with the intention of selling the Rockcliffe property. Offers are being received for the Rockcliffe property.

From whom-private
parties?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Private people, syndicates and the like. The question of disposing of a property of that kind is a difficult one for a government. A government cannot -very well get into the real estate business. In order to get the full value out of that property it has to be divided and subdivided. It will probably have to be sold in small sections over a period of time, and a government cannot do that very well. The same thing applies'to the beautiful property at Toronto known as the Rifle Range property. The hon, member for Victoria (Sir Sam Hughes) says it

should be kept as a rifle range. It is a property valued at between $1,500 and $2,000 an acre and there are between 500 and 600 acres. It is far too valuable to be used as a rifle range. It is bounded on the north by the provincial highway and on the south by lake Ontario, and all around it are the highest-class residential buildings in Ontario. It is not suitable for a rifle range. How to dispose of it is the question. The Government has not yet determined how it is going to do it.

I hope the minister will
not think of disposing of the Long Branch ranges property until he has another one in sight. That property is supposed to be a very good range. The Provincial Rifle Association meets there every year, and the range also supplies facilities for practice for the regiments at Toronto where there are the best shots in Canada. Land is pretty expensive all over, but I hope the minister will not think of selling our only rifle range unless he has another suitable property to substitute for it.

First of all, the Militia Department had a very valuable property in the western part of Toronto known as the Garrison Common. That property was obtained by the Militia Department from the Imperial Government. An arrangement was made whereby it was to be sold to the city of Toronto and the Toronto Exhibition Association in lieu of land which the city and the Exhibition Association were to purchase for the department. The city and the Exhibition Association purchased land out near the Humber so that the Stanley barracks could be moved there. The permanent force was to be established on this property. The rifle Tange was purchased out on the Lake Shore road originally for the purpose of the riflemen and for the use of the Ontario Rifle Association. They used to lease to the Ontario Rifle Association the old Garrison Common. The Government bought this new rifle range near Port Credit and the militia units used it and the Ontario Rifle Association. Subsequently the Government disposed, at a big profit, of the land at the Humber, making a few hundred thousand dollars on the transaction, and they purchased a cheap property alongside of the -rifle range where it was the intention to establish the new barracks for the permanent force. When the minister says that there is going to be a new policy and that this land is going to be sold, the city of Toronto will certainly ask some questions. It will want to know

where the permanent force is going to be located. As a matter of fact, the Stanley barracks, where the permanent force is located to-day, belongs to the city of Toronto and there is no reason why the permanent force should be allowed to remain ther.e a day longer. The city of Toronto bought that property and paid for it but the permanent force is still there. It is not the property of the Militia Department any longer in so far as fairness and equity are concerned, because the city of Toronto has satisfied the Militia Department by giving it a property to take the place of the Garrison Common property. Where is the permanent force going to be located if you are going to do away with the property at Long Branch? Where are you going to get, in the vicinity of Toronto, a rifle range that will meet the requirements of the present long-range rifle? You will have to go out fifteen or twenty miles unless you are prepared to pay twice as much as you will get for the Lake Shore road land. I had the opportunity of going over topographical surveys and plans of rifle ranges within fifteen or twenty miles of Toronto and there was only one that I could see that was within any reasonable distance of Toronto. Before that policy is adopted the Militia Department had better, to use a current expression, mind its step, because it is not going to act fairly or justly if it does what the minister suggests.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Does my hon. friend know the attitude of Toronto in reference to this matter because we have had communication with them?

I do npt know the attitude of the city of Toronto, but I know the attitude of the citizens of Toronto. If the minister accepts the attitude< of two or three aldermen in the city of Toronto he is liable to err. Their attitude in regard to the rifle range cannot be taken as that of the city. The council of the city of Toronto is made up in part of real estate dealers who, very likely, want to see the rifle range sold so that it can subsequently be disposed of in lots. I do not know' where there is any other land within a reasonable distance of the city and I am sure the ex-Minister of Militia (Sir Sam Hughes) will bear me out in that. This is the first time that anybody ever heard the council or anybody else in Toronto wanting to remove the permanent force, sell the rifle range and not build the barracks out at Long Branch.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
We must not have any misunderstanding about this. I did speak
of removing the permanent force but of establishing it in Toronto. There is nothing to house the permanent force at the present rifle range property. The huts are there, but they are largely blown down. We have transferred the old Garrison Commons to the city of Toronto, and we are there now as tenants-at-will of the city. The city does not want to put us out, and we want to find a suitable place in Toronto. We have a property in Rosedale, but there is great objection to our utilizing it for barracks. We have the St. Andrew's College property which we bought during the war for $500,000, and we want to dispose of it. We are sure we can get a little more than that for it now. We have that property worth $1,500 or $2,000 an acre in the finest residential part of the city of Toronto, and to use that for a barracks would be rather extravagant. Consequently another site will have to be provided. We do not want to keep the old Stanley barracks; it is not suitable and there are complaints in regard to it. The officers of the Toronto district have gone into this question from top to bottom but the difficulty is where to locate. Detachments of men who should be stationed in Toronto to-day are not there. The Princess Patricias are in London whereas they ought to be in Toronto. I do not know whether we shall be able to move them this year to Toronto or not. We have in the Orthopedic Hospital a very large building, but the units in Toronto want it for ordinary drill hall purposes. In any event it will take a lot of money to make it suitable for barracks. It is a difficult problem that confronts us. The idea was to get a new rifle range if one could be secured, and establish a new barracks in Toronto. The question of the money was not the difficulty, in view of the valuable property we hold.
Why not use part of the rifle range for the barracks?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: There is room' there, but in the first place I think it is pretty valuable land to use for establishing a barracks and in the second place the objection from headquarters in Toronto is that it is nine miles from the City Hall and the main objection is the time consumed in getting from one place to another; the amount of travelling is too great, and then there is the question of expense.
Is it too far from the pink teas?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
It is the men that are
making the complaint, not the officers.

I know something about
this question and I think I ought to say a word or two about it. The present barracks, I think, are to small, and the officers cannot get recruits, especially for the permanent force, unless the barracks accommodation is made better. You see, our young fellows in Canada are accustomed to the conveniences of life, and to living in good houses. They are not going into a ramshackle barracks where ten or twelve men occupy one room and there is no privacy. Unless the Government can find its way to provide barracks accommodation such as they have in the Old Country and in the United States-where the dwellings are really homes for the men and they take a pride in them-it is going to experience difficulty in getting recruits. I know perfectly well the Government is up against great difficulty in getting accommodation at this time; but if you take the men out nine miles from the city where they cannot get in to see the motion pictures, or to visit their friends, and that kind of thing, it militates against recruiting. The thing to do now is to try and secure barracks within a reasonable distance of the centres of amusement, and shops, and similar conveniences, otherwise the men will not enlist.
I am sorry to say I have to
10 p.in. somewhat resent the character of the remarks made by the hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. Currie). That hon. member characterized the aider-men of Toronto in a way that is not acceptable to me. He must remember, although he comes from North Simcoe, that these transactions are not left to one or two aldermen, but that anything that is done is done by the city council as a whole -a very respectable body of men, who never take any action without great deliberation.

With regard to this matter I wish to say that when the land was purchased at Long Branch for the permanent force, as an addition to the rifle range, plans and specifications were prepared-in fact I think tenders were called just at the outbreak of the war-in order to put up these barracks. Nothing further in that direction was done, but for the last two or three years there have been mysterious purchases of land in the vicinity of Toronto for military purposes. The reason for these transactions is not apparent but everybody knows that the Militia Department have made enough money out of the transactions in land in Toronto to have built these barracks and to have built them

long ago. As far as the city council of Toronto is concerned I do not think this matter ever came before them.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
No, we have decided
not to put the barracks there. That was why we entered into negotiations with the city of Toronto. We have abandoned the idea of building barracks in Rosedale, but we have that property now and we have to dispose of it. The question we are trying to settle is a suitable location for a barracks in Toronto, but any negotiations that have taken place have been purely informal, and there has been no offer.
To whom?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
There have been no
agreements. All we have been doing has been casting about with the idea of locating the most convenient place for a barracks to be put.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Nothing of the kind will take place. I earn give my hon. friend an assurance of that.
I presume that, as the hon. member for North Simcoe says, there is question of land speculation involved.
Real estate.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I can assure my hon. friend that nothing of the kind will be done without the fullest inquiry and the widest publicity and without proper regard for the interests of all concerned.
The minister stated a moment agioi that he intended to sell the Dorval property. Has any report been miade which would indicate that the sale of that property is justifiable?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: IMy hon. friend must not put words in my mouth. I did not say that I intended to sell any property. What I said was that the policy was now under consideration of selling such properties as were not being utilized. I afn told that there is some objection to .the Dorval property. I understand that for one thing, the level of the land is below the level of the river. I do not know how true that is, but if it is true it would be a serious defect. But I am not at all familiar with the Dorval property; I have never seen it.

I remember that when the property was purchased a ifew years ago the transaction was criticised, but it was very hotly defended on the floor of the House. The property was represented as being .a good one, very accessible to the militiamen of Montreal. Niow we are informed that it is below the level of the St. Lawrence.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: If the property is as suitable as my hon. friend thinks it is, it may be adopted as a site. I understand that there lare objections to it.
Has my hon. friend any report .against that property, or any report to justify his assertion that it may be sold?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I have simply made the general statement that the question of the sale of all military property in Canada which is not being utilized is under consideration. My information is that the Dorval property is not being utilized. If it should turn out that the Dorval property is suitable for barracks I ck* not see .any reason for selling it; but if it is unsuitable and not being used for militia purposes there is every reason for not holding it, provided a proper price can be obtained for it.

I chance to know a little .about the Dorval property. There is mo truth whatever in the statement that it is beloiw the level of the river. The Canadian Pacific and the Grand Trunk Railway lines run through it. The plans are in the department to-day, or were there when I left, for the septic tanks for draining the property. At time of high ice flood the property has had water on it, the same as parts of Montreal itself have had water on them in days gone by, but there is no more danger of the place being under water than there is of the city of Ottawa where we mow stand being under water. [DOT] The property is quite a suitable property, the

only place we could get within reasonable distance of Montreal. Officers and noncommissioned officers were consulted with regard to the purchase of the property; it was generally regarded as a very suitable site and as the .most convenient place for officers to train for their certificates. If plans were taken of the militia properties that were handed over by the Imperial Government in the various cities and centres throughout Canada and a comparison made of the extent of those properties and that of the properties which we now have, the public would be startled. There was the case of Lafontaine park in Montreal, which was handed over for a song. My policy was to hold to every foot of land we had. These properties do not cost the country anything for maintenance and they are all coming in handy. The whole trouble is that a number of speculators get after the Government in one form or another, and the first thing you know is that these properties are sold and then the Government has to turn round and pay large sums for other property. Keep the speculator out of this business and things will come out all right.
Alongside the Doirval property there is a remount station. Is that owned by the department or is it only leased?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I believe that it was leased by the Imperial Government. I do not know whether or not it is in existence now. It does not belong to this Government.
Is it the intention of the Government to remove the Ross Rifle factory from the Plains of Abraham?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I really never heard that question discussed, but I will take it up and consider it. I do not really know enough about it to answer.

Last year the minister's predecessor had given the matter consideration hut evidently had not reached any conclusion. It is 'a very important matter and the people of the city of Quebec v'ould be grateful for any information that the minister can give on t'he subject.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
The hon. member for Quebec AVest (Mr. Parent) spoke to me once on the subject and I think I said that we might go down- and look the situation over. But I Teally have not any information on the subject. I can make in

quirias 'and will give my hon. friend an answer.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext:
On motion of Hon. Martin Burrell (Minister of Customs -and Inland Revenue) Bill No. 167, to amend 'the Post Office Act, was read the second time, -and the House went into committee 'thereon, Mr. Boivtin in the Chair.
On section 1-maximum registration fee increased from five to ten cents:

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What is the meaning of that amendment?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: Under the present registration fee of five cents the department has been losing about -a quarter of a million dollars annually, and this loss will be augmented toy increases of salaries, 'and so on. We 'are now placing the fee for registration *at ten cents instead of five. That is the same as they have it in the United States -and lower than the registration fee in England. The rural postmasters will obtain slightly increased remuneration on account Of the increased revenue.
What is the rate of domestic postage in the United States?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: Two cents.
Then for registered letters we will have to pay the ordinary postage of three cents and an additional ten cents, a total of thirteen cents. Does the minister consider that reasonable?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: Of course, the extra cent on the ordinary postage is an increase made on account of the war expenditures, so we might leave that out of consideration. But the registration fee in the United States is, as we are proposing, namely, ten cents.

As the
domestic postage there is two cents, our rate should be the same. Surely we are not behind the United 'States in that matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: We are well up to them anyway.

This is an increase of
100 per cent, and it is a pretty quick jump. We have surely enough taxes to pay without this one. If we want to send a registered letter, that costs ten cenlts; special delivery costs ten cents, and then there is a war tax in addition on domestic postage.
We want some explanation.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue

speechtext:
The minister says that
this is to cover a loss on registered mail. Surely there cannot be a loss of one hundred per cent on registered mail. The revenue of the department surely cannot be only fifty per cent of the expenditure on registered mail. There is only Ithe stationery required, and the time required by the clerk to register, and the cost of the postage stamp. A special bag may be required, hut does the department pay anything extra to the railway companies or other carriers for carrying registered mail?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue

speechtext:
Why not make the rate
eight cents?

What is
the total deficit in the Post Office Department for the past year?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: I cannot give my hon. friend the exact figures in relation to the Post Office Department, but practically the war revenue and the additional one-cent postage wiped out the deficit.
Do I understand there was no deficit at all last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: No deficit last year.
Then, what is Ithe purpose of increasing this rate on registered mail?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
We cannot say that
there will not be a deficit next year.
Is the increase being made in anticipation of a deficit this year?

The Government ought
to increase the rates on the railways also if that be the case. I understand this is to cover a deficit or because there is a shortage in revenue. This increase of five cents must be based on something. Surely it is not a haphazard guess made by officials of the department to increase the revenue. It must be for the purpose of meeting a deficiency in revenue, and it must toe based on certain data. I should presume that that data would toe a deficit or shortage in revenue in the Post Office Department. My hon. friend (Mr. Burrell), acting for the Postmaster General, says that the one-cent war tax covers the deficit they had in the department, and without knowing what the probable deficit may be next year, we are going to charge an additional five cents. If we take the past year as a basis, this five cents additional is going to be a net surplus, or we might say that it is a disguised war tax that is being imposed by the Post Office Department instead of being imposed by the Finance Department. If there be no deficit, why charge this five cents additional? If there be a deficit, why not charge just ehough to cover the difference between the revenue and expenditure of this branch of the Post Office Department?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue

speechtext:
What constitutes the
additional expense in the registration branch? I understand, of course, there must be a registration branch in every post office, but in the bulk of the post offices throughout the country, the postmaster who

receives a small salary looks after the registration branch as well.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: There are various expenses, administration, equipment, bags, different handling and a large increase in the number of employees in comparison with a general post office.

If the minister will allow me before he replies, I should like to complete a statement I made a moment ago regarding the reorganization of the department under the direction of the German-American firm. I forgot to mention that we have, from the Government themselves, the admission that very important reductions in the expenditure can be made through the inspection which will take place and which probably might render it unnecessary to impose a new tax on the people of Canada. This is what the Government states in this report:
The Company is ot the opinion, and the Committee-
That is, the Committee of the Privy Council.



-sees no reason for disagreeing therewith, that commencing the reorganization of these two departments, savings will begin to be realized gradually after two or three months of work, which, in the end, in respect to the Post Office Department, may well reach many hundreds of thousands of dollars per year, with proportionate savings in the Customs Department, and the Committee believes that based upon the results already obtained, and the expenditure already made in respect to the classification of the whole Civil Service and the reorganization of the one branch which has now been nearly completed, it is wise, if not imperative, that the work should be carried on and the benefits extended gradually to the other Departments.
I am not passing judgment on the advisability of entrusting the reorganization of the department to foreigners. I am not discussing that phase of the question; that is another point altogether. But I say that the Government themselves admit that when this reorganization takes place under the direction of that firm hundreds of thousands of dollars per annum will be saved in the Post Office Department. If that result can be attained within a few months, as it is stated in the report of the Privy Council, why should we let the poor public pay in advance? My hon. friend should postpone this proposed taxation; and first of all, as charity begins at home, he should reduce expenditures, thus preventing the public of this country from paying for the follies of the department.
The domestic rate there is reduced to two cents.

The registration fee was raised to ten cents and that rate is still in force. It is true the postal rate has been reduced from three to two cents, but their financial situation is not the same as it is in. Canada.

Was not the money all put into the post office fund and used for the purpose of running the post office? One of the complaints on the part of the public is that this one-cent tariff was put on for a war tax and that it was never used for war purposes. It was used for the post office.
All these revenues are put into the consolidated revenue fund,, the cost of the operation of the department is paid and the accounts go through the Auditor General's hands.
That is quite true but- the consolidated, revenue fund did not pay the war.

The money from the Post Office Department went into the consolidated * revenue fund, and if we had not put on that extra cent of war tax we would have had a deficit of at least $4,000,000 or $5,000,000. The annual statement, as read by the hou. member for Miaisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux), was to the effect that the cost of administreing the department had increased'.
More than doubled.
The hon. member for Guysboirough cam see that if we had not had this $4,000,000 or $5,000,000 we would not have had sufficient money for the operation of the department.

There is another matter to which I wish to call the attention of the minister and that is the sale of postage stamps for inland revenue purposes. I understand the proceeds from the sale of these stamps is credited to the Post Office Department, whereas the stamps are used for inland revenue purposes. I raised that point a year ago and the minister in charge of the Bill assured me that the money would be credited to inland revenue during the year. Does the Post Office Department receive credit for the sale of postage stamps that are used for inland revenue purposes?	'

I remember that some one-'perhaps it was the hon. gentleman- asked last year why we should not have a separate stamp for inland revenue purposes. The answer was that it would be very inconvenient in outlying districts if you had to have one stamp for the inland revenue tax and a different one for postage. The Postmaster General and his staff have stated that it is absolutely impossible to keep them separate or to say how much has been paid for inland revenue purposes and how much has been paid for post office.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: I am not at all sure that I can give my hon. friend the information he wants, because it is a postage stamp that is used. I could give him the figure's in regard to the inland revenue stamps, but in regard to postage stamps that the public are allowed to use for inland revenue purposes, it would be impossible to tell where the division comes. I would be very glad, when we come to the Inland Revenue Estimates to give him the figures of the inland revenue stamps. We know it is a great convenience to the public to allow them to use postage stamps. I suppose the system was established for that purpose and as a matter of public convenience.
Is the committee to understand that the entire receipts from the sale of postage stamps are all credited to the Post Office Department and are used to defray the cost of carrying on that department?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: They all go to the credit of the Receiver General, I presume, through the Post Office Department.
Then it follows that the Post Office Department gets credit for a large amount of money from the sale of postage stamps that it is no tentitled to.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: Yes, I think there is no doubt something in what my hon. friend says. My hon. friend from Bonaventure (Mr. March) asked me in regard to the figures.
The figures of the registration division.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
I gave them the other
night when Ithe resolutions were being considered. At all events I said that the total revenue was about half a million dollars and the total ,cost of administration about three-quarters of a million and will be more this year on account of the great increase in salaries and so on.

Mr. MARiCIL:	Has there been any increase in remuneration to Ithe country postmasters at all?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: I believe that is under consideration alt the present time. This legislation will incidentally affect the country postmasters; it will give them more revenue because their salaries are based on the business done.
Is the commission paid the postmasters with respect to registration stamps the same as in .other cases?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: The same commission.
Has the minister nothing to say about the firm to which reference has been made?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
Well, I cannot tell my hon. friend much about the firm. I think it is a branch of the same firm that has done work in connection with the reorganization of the Bureau, and they have been selected upon the advice and recommend-altion of tlio Civil Service Commission. I have watched their work very closely, and I do not think my hon. friend is perhaps quite fair to them. They are no doubt men of great business efficiency and have made a special study of these matters. I think anybody who has waltched the work done in the reorganization of the Bureau will probably admit that it has been put in a businesslike condition that will mean an immense annual saving to the country, and wilth probably just as efficient results as regards production. Whatever my hon. friend may say about the Post Office Department, I do not think there is a man in this House-and I can say this certainly from a non-partisan standpoint-but will admit that the introdudtion of modern methods of business into a department of Government here or elsewhere would accomplish a great deal. But fit is difficult work and may arouse a lot off friction. I am not going to pronounce on this particular firm except to say that those who have had Ithe opportunity of judging their work and who have read the report of the Civil Service Commission believe that they are well equipped for suoh duties, and will render good service to the public and to the country.
Mr. A. R. M'CjMAiSIIvR (Brome) (Translation) :	Mr. Chairman, we have to-night a
very- sad spectacle. The postmaster is not here in this House, he is in the Senate, and we have no opportunity to examine his budget, or rather his bill. We have an
fMr. Burrell.]
amiable gentleman, who does not know much about the matter before the House, and he is in difficulties; he calls out for help, and the minister who shoulders the largest deficit answers his call. But he is again in difficulties and then comes another member of the Government, a gentleman with a cunning smile, who gives his precious help to both of his colleagues; but the three of them, who may be compared to the Musketeers so much talked of in the novels .otf Victor Hugo

Mr. LAPiO.BNT'E: Alexandre Dumas.
Well, Alexandre Dumas, they do not see the difference. These three gentlemen together are not worth one member from Gaspe and Maisonneuve, when he was minister of the department.

Apart from the fact that it has been stated in this memorandum from the Privy Council that there are 24,000 employees in the Post Office Department and that very material reductions should be made within a very short time thus saving several hundred thousand dollars. I wish to call the attention of my hon. friend -who I know is British-born and must stand by British parliamentary precedents -to the fact that if there is one thing for which I have great regard, if there is anything for which I admire the British people, it is their love for free parliamentary institutions. I say that this is a very serious departure from parliamentary government, from responsible government. The ministers are responsible to Parliament and Parliament is responsible to the people. Now you are departing absolutely from the old time-honoured principle that the ministers shall direct their own departments, and for the administration of those departments will be responsible to Parliament itself. Now the ministers will remain idle, will eat the bread of idleness, and they w'ill shift their work to commissions. If the commissions appointed were even British or Canadian I would object, but not so strenuously as I do object when I see these super-loyal ministers of the Crown in the Unionist Government shifting their task to German-American firms. I say it is a great blot on the Canadian escutcheon, it is a great stricture on parliamentary traditions, to thus shift your work onto foreign commissions and get them to investigate your departments. But apart from the parliamentary and traditional point of view, how is it that the Govern-

ment in their new departure, have first selected the Post Office Department for investigation? Is that not clear evidence that there is "something rotten in the state of Denmark"? Is there not in that very fact, and the bringing in of German-Amer-ican firms, to first investigate the Post Office Department, evidence that the ministers who, since 1911, have been the presiding and responsible heads of that department have failed, and lamentably failed, in their duty? I leave it to you Mr. Chairman: Will you believe that any miii-ister in the -Post Office Department could defend the doubling, and more than doubling, of the expenditure in the department as compared with a time when we had a better service? Although it is very sad to have to impose new forms of taxation upon the public, I am rather pleased to find that whereas under a straight Liberal Government we had a surplus, notwithstanding a reduction of postal taxation under the Tory-Unionist Government, despite an increase of taxation, there is a deficit. The comparison need not be elaborated, I leave it at that. My only regret is that the smiling minister is here to bear the white man's burden. But there is no white man in the case I am sorry to say; there are many niggers on the fence in the department, from what I know. I am only sorry my hon. friend is here in this House bearing the burden of another minister who has not yet once given this House the benefit of his experience as Postmaster General. Since 1911 no Postmaster General has given an account of his stewardship; yet to-night we have this spectacle: three ministers of the Crown cannot explain the serious gap which exists as between the figures of 1911 and 1920. Yet the people of the country are being subjected to increased taxation.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
I do not think I ought
to let pass without comment my hon. friend's remark about the placing of ministerial responsibility in the hands of somebody who is not responsible. As I understand it, the Government are just as responsible in connection with any work which this firm may do in the matter of reorganization as they would be , if it were being done through their own deputies or their own officers.

With this difference:
that you pay $10,000 a month for that work, while ministers of the Crown are paid by the State to do it, and they have 24,000 employees in the department to carry out their instructions.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: My hon. friend is skipping the point. The extent of parliamentary responsibility is exactly the same in the one case as in the other. My hon. friend may cherish his own opinion as to the value of the work in question, but the point of parliamentary responsibility is there just the same. My hon. friend says that I am bearing somebody else's burden. Well, I suppose we all have to bear one another's burdens; it is part of our work in life. But I wish to point out, as my hon. friend seems to be fearfully distressed about the Postmaster General being in the Senate, that during the fifteen years that the Liberal administration was in power there were times when no less than thre ministers were members of the Senate. At different times, under the administration of Sir Wilfrid Laurier and in prior administrations, members of the Government holding the port folios of Agriculture, Trade and Commerce. Justice, and I think, one or two others, were in the Senate. That question also may be arguable, but I do not think my hon. friend should press it too far. Of course, if he wants to move for the abolition of the Senate, that is another matter.
May I inquire whether these experts will try their hand at the re-organization of the Union Government as well?
The minister said that he expected great saving in the Post Office Department as a result of this re-organization. In what way does he expect to bring about that saving?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
I do not think my hon. friend can reasonably expect me to go into the details of a scheme that has practically not yet been worked out. But to put it in a broad way, I would say that throughout all government departments, in this country as well as in the United States, and possibly in England,, there do grow up under all our political systems accretions to the public service that are not altogether based on efficiency. We know what has happened in the past, and in that respect we need not place the blame upon one party more than another. All sorts of men and women have been placed in the service; some are kept on that should not be kept on; the equipment is not always kept up-to-date or as a modern business house would keep its equiment. Then there are such matters as methods of arrangement in regard to the department itself, actual physical facilities, and that kind of thing. All these matters are open to improvement, in modern offices with modern methods. I do not think my hon.

friend would expect me to say what particular lines the re-organization will take.

I suggest to the minister that he advise his colleague, the Postmaster General, to remain in Ottawa instead of going into constituencies where there are by-elections, and thus save money to the country. In 1917 there was a by-election in my county. A gentleman by the name of Hon. Mr. Sevigny was running'. The present Postmaster General came down and as a colleague of the minister who represents him to-night he opened no less than three post offices the day before polling took place. No wonder we have deficits in the Post Office Department. Everybody knows that the minister is and always has been absolutely incompetent; he never showed competency anywhere. If the Government want to bring about real reform in the Civil Service they ought to substitute someone else for the present Postmaster General. He represents nobody. He was defeated in two counties in the province of Quebec, losing his deposit in both; yet he is imposed upon us by this Government as representative of our province in the Cabinet. We do not want it. He cannot stay in the House because he cannot secure election, but through a bargain that everybody knows of he has been appointed to the Senate. How can the people of Canada have confidence in a department administered by such a minister? The burden of representing him on this occasion is on my hon. friend (Mr. Burrell); he feels it and we all feel it and that is why we sympathize with him. The hon. gentleman says: let us increase the fee for registration of mail matter before economizing in the department. Always the same method, Mr. Chairman,-let the ordinary, common people pay for the extravagance of the head of the department. There is an economy which suggests itself to everybody-remove the minister himself and save $7,000 which he does not earn. The Postmaster General of Canada to-day has absolutely nothing to do in the direction of the Post Office Department. When a strike takes place in Vancouver, Winnipeg or Toronto it is the President of the Council (Mr. Rowell) who settles those strikes-or unsettles them, or it is the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) who goes to Winnipeg in that connection. The Postmaster General does nothing. Why is he there? Cut out his salary and save $7,000; remove him from the Senate and savft another $2,500, and close the useless post offices which were opened everywhere. Cancel the contracts at

exorbitant prices which were given to friends by the Government of the day, Have an auction of those famous padlocks, the contract for which was given to my hon. friend as an inheritance by the Hon. Mr. Pelletier. As the minister may see, many reforms could be effected in the Post Office Department. Why impose new taxes? Why ask the people to pay more when it is so easy to reform and economise in other ways? We, of * the Opposition, do not hold these three ministers responsible; they do not know anything about the department. If it takes' three ministers in this House to defend the Postmaster General, I am not surprised that the Postmaster General is satisfied to remain in the Senate and not to come here himself. But the people of Canada will not be satisfied with any legislation introduced to increase the burden of taxation existing at present, when the department is not administered in a satisfactory way and by a minister who is responsible to the people, but is administered by a minister who, as I said, represents absolutely nothing.
Mr. MicKENZIE: The Post Office Department, iif a registered letter is lost, reimburses the loss to the extent of $20 or $25. That was the case when the ordinary registration fee of five oents was charged. Now that a man has to pay ten cents, will he have any guarantee as to larger sums sent through the mail?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: The present practice is to make good a loss up to $25. My hon. friend is asking whether there would be a greater amount guaranteed if the rate is increased to ten cents. The amount would be left the same as it is to-day.

The Minister of Railways (Mr. J. D. Reid), in speaking on this subject rather intimated that the loading up of the department was due to the deputy minister of the department and his officials. The minister in charge of the Bill (Mr Burrell) softened that a little by saying that it was the custom during Tory Governments to overload the departments. Which of the ministers are we to take as the authority and to believe, on this subject? Does the fault in regard to this overmanning of the department lie with the minister in charge or with the officials?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
In the first place, I did not understand the Minister of Railways to refer to the loading up of the department. I understood him to say that the largely in-

creased, expenditures were due to necessary increases of expenses 'everywhere, such as railway rates, steamship rates, equipment, wages, salaries and son on. During the war I suppose the expense was pretty heavy because, speaking from memory, I think something like 2,000-there may have been more-post office employees went to the war who, under .an arrangement which was made when they enlisted, were paid, not only the pay of their rank, but their salaries. All those things contributed to the increased expense. I think we would all probably agree that every department could be carried on with fewer employees if it were brought up thoroughly to modern business requirements. I am not casting the blame for that on one side or the other. It is manifest to everyone that this state of affairs exists to a greater or less extent. We would ail welcome an improvement, and there is no necessity of making a party question out of the -matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
Answering that in a
broad way and speaking for myself, I would say that I would not increase my staff unless it were Shown to me by my -responsible officials that employees -were needed for a special purpose; or if a department launching out into new avenues of work, if it were clearly .shown that we .required more employees. I think the question could be answered generally in that way.

Would it be possible for the Civil .Service Commission to deal with the reorganization of the department without employing outside help? The members of the Civil Service Commission, no doubt, have had a certain amount of experience during the time they have been in charge of reclassification, and if they are the capable men I presume they are, with the knowledge they have gained during the time they have been in control of these matters, I would say, as a man of somp experience in handling employees, that these men should be capable of dealing with the situation without bringing in outside help. That would save the expense of bringing in these men from another country to investigate the working and operations of our departments; and to say the least, in my judgment, it is inadvisable to put these foreigners., as they are, in possession of facts and inside information regarding the operations of various departments of the Civil Service of this country. If the Civil Service Commission are not capable of dealing with the situation, we should be able to find in Canada men who are capable of .conducting that investigation.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: il think my hon. friend would see that with the number of civil servants in Canada-and I should say the number was not less than 50,000 or GO,000 in all services-and with the work that falls on the Civil Service Commission at the present time, it would be impossible for them to go personally into details of organization of different departments. My hon. friend would only have to visit the Civil Service .Commission for a day or so and see their work to realise that. As I understand the matter, although this question would probably be better dealt with on the Estimates of the department, this firm would go into the matter with the co-operation of certain officials selected in the various departments, so that the work would be one of co-operation.

Does the minister think it advisable to bring from a foreign country men to inquire into a matter of this character when no doubt they will obtain regarding the operation of various departments information which I do not think the Government should allow to be in the possession of any men from a foreign country?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
The commission were
authorised to engage such expert services as they -could secure to do this work of organisation that they have been doing during the last year or so, and especially the work of reorganizing the Printing Bureau. On that authorisation they secured the best experts they could find; they made a recommendation to the Government, and the Government thought fit to accept their recommendation.
/

Earlier in the session I took upon myself to express my views in regard to the appointment of this Arthur Young Company in connection with the re-classifi-eation of the Civil Service. At that time I thought I had made it plain that the services which this firm and their employees were rendering to this Government and the country were very much over-estimated. It seems that the Government does not take the advice of those like myself who have some special knowledge of these matters, but has undertaken to re-employ' a certain section of the same firm employed on that re-classification. I submit that it is impossible to discuss the item before the Chair without also discussing the remedy which the Government proposes to put into effect, namely, a supposed or contemplated reduction in the expenditure of the department by reason of this reorganization. I desire to place myself on record as of the opinion that the employment of these gentlemen is absolutely unjustifiable and cannot be defended either in this House or outside. The apparent reason for it is a supposed saving in the reorganization of the Printing Bureau. Now it is ludicrous to any one who understands the real inside working of the Printing Bureau to hear the President of the Privy Council say, as he did in a speech delivered a short time ago in this House, that the splendid work done by these gentlemen in the Printing Bureau was going to save this country-I think he said had already saved this country-'$400,000. Why, that is a myth, an absolute myth. If you take into consideration the value of the machinery which these gentlemen have despoiled and the expensive machinery which they have ordered, and add up the cost you will find that instead of there being a saving to this country there will be a loss at the end of twelve months. I have had occasion to in- < terview some practical men employed in the Bureau and they tell me that the statement I have made is absolutely correct. It seems to me the Government ought to call a halt on employing men of the calibre of Mr. Wolff, who is the boss in charge at the Printing Bureau at the present time, and who does not take his orders from this Government or from any officials of this Government. It was only the other day,
I am informed on very creditable authority, that a minister gave an order for certain work to be performed outside the Bureau and this German-American, Mr. Wolff, when it was brought to his attention, very arrogantly expressed the opinion that he did not take his orders from the minister 
of that department or anybody else, that he was in charge of the work at the Printing Bureau. Yet it is proposed by this Government to continue the services of these gentlemen, at $10,000 a month or more-
Plus expenses.

-to do what the head of
the department ought to be able to do himself. If the Deputy Postmaster General, after his twehty-odd years in the department, is- not in a position to reorganize it and reduce the staff, if there are more employees than are required, he ought not to hold that office. W'hy is it necessary to bring in some American gentleman to reorganize a department in which we have an officer who ought to be better acquainted with its workings than any outsider could possibly be in twelve months? It cannot be justified, and I would not be doing justice to myself nor to the constituency that I have the honour to represent if I did not say so. I know perhaps as well as, if not better than, most hon. gentlemen of this House the position of the Civil Service, whether it is overmanned or not, and I venture to say this: If the King's Printer, or the Assistant King's Printer, had been ordered by this Government to reorganize the Printing Bureau they would have reorganized it just as efficiently, if not more so, than these gentlemen did at an expenditure to this country of $200,000. The difficulty is the Government does not say to the heads of the different departments: We think you are overmanned and that you should reduce your staff. I venture to say that every deputy minister is just as anxious to have efficiency in his department as the Government is. I venture to say further that every deputy minister resents, and properly so, the bringing into their department of outside gentlemen, men who are not 'Canadian, and who say "John Smith is incompetent" and "William Jones is competent," without even consulting the deputy minister's opinion as to that particular person's ability to do his work. If our deputy ministers and the chiefs of their branches are not capable of reorganizing their respective departments and it is necessary to go outside, then I submit it is proper that some good Canadians just as well qualified as these American gentlemen should have been employed for that purpose.

speechtext:
The clause under consideration reads as follows:
Paragraph (k) of subsection one of section nine of the Post Office Act, Revi.se'l Statutes of

Canada, 1'9'0'6, chapter sixty-six, as amended by chapter twenty-nine of the statutes of 1909, is amended by substituting the word "ten" for the word "five" in the seventh line thereof.
This clause provides for the increase of the rat<= on registered letters from 5 to 10 cents. Subsection 5 of Rule 13 says:
Speeches in Committee of the Whole must be strictly relevant to the item or clause under consideration.
In view of that rule, and the clause before the committee, I certainly must decide that-any discussion concerning the 'reorganization of the public service at the Printing Bureau or elsewhere, or any contemplated reorganization of the public service is not in order. It may be argued by some hon. members that the entire Bill is a Bill to increase post office rates for the purpose of meeting a deficit and that the reorganization of the Post Office Department is germane to the issue. Even if this argument was correct the discussion could only take place when the principle of the Bill was being considered at the time of its second reading. The principle of the Bill has been adopted, and this debate is certainly not in order upon the consideration of any individual clause. ,

I do not wish, Mr. Chairman, to question your ruling, but it seems to me that when by means of a Bill a new from of taxation is proposed in one department, it is our right to demonstrate that by cutting down the expenditure in that department the taxation would not be necessary. That was the object of this discussion. We were not discussing the reorganization of the department, but have stated that the Department was being investigated, and that in the Order in Council appointing this firm it was stated that several hundreds of thousands of dollars would be saved by the reorganization of the Post Office Department which was overmanned. We were simply showing that there was inordinate expenditure in that department, and that the public should not be called upon to pay for the mal- ad ministration of the Government.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I understand perfectly the nature of the discussion. My hon. friend would be quite right if this discussion had taken place on the second reading of the Bill when the principle of increased taxation in the Post - Office Department was at issue. But it certainly is not in order when we are considering individual clauses of the Bill,
when the speeches must be strictly relevant to the clause under consideration.
Mr. GLASS * In the earlier part of the evening the hon. member for Maison-neuve was drawing attention to the large increase in the expenditure of the Post Office Department, and pointing out that in his opinion this increase in ;the rate of registration was partly due to a desire to make up a deficit in the revenues of the Post Office Department. He also pointed out that the increase in the cost of administration of the department was not justified by the increase in our population. In my opinion it is not so much an increase in population as in the general business of the country that affects the expenditure of the department. We know that in the Dominion of Canada between the years my hon. friend mentioned, 1911 and the present time, the manufacturing products of this country increased from $1,500,000 to over $3,000,000. We also know by the deposits and general business of our banks that there has been an increase in the business of the country in that time of more than 100 per cent. That, of itself, would mean a large increase in the service and an increased cost. The Minister of Railways has pointed out some of the factors that enter into the increased cost of the administration, one of which is the development of the rural mail service. The hon. member for Maison-neuve (Mr. Lemieux) stated justly that he instituted this service in Canada, hut I submit that when he resigned the administration of the department this service was a very insignificant branch of the Post Office Department compared with that. which exists to-day. Apart from that, the large increase in wages, which have more than doubled since his time, would necessarily account to a great extent for the general increase. No one expects, and we have not looked for, a large revenue or profit from the administration of this department. Tt is a public utility which is administered to a large extent at a loss.
I question if there is a 'Solitary Tural mail service, in the country, the revenues derived from which are sufficient to pay for the cost of that particular route. There is a loss all through. I wish to point oiut to the committee a fact which, in my opinion, has a great significance. Let us take the United States with its large population. I have before me the figures in connection with the cost of the administration of the Post Office Department of the United States

from the time of the Civil War down to 1913. The whole total of the revenues from 1866 to 1913 amounted to $3,775,000,000, and the total cost of operation in that time amounted to $4,555,000,000. Now, Mr. Chairman, in that time that country with its immense population, and a greater opportunity far making a profit in this connection if .a profit were possible-during a great part of the time I have mentioned they collected a three-cent instead of a two-cent rate-sustained a loss in the administration of the Post Office Department of $800,000,000. Let us study the subject somewhat closely. I shall take the period from the year 1884 to 1913. .Mark you, in 1884 the population of the United States was approximating ninety millions and in ' the last decade a hundred millions. But notwithstanding this, during the thirty years immediately preceding 1913 the total deficit in the administration of the Post Office Department in the United States amounted to $210,000,000. Now, iSir, let me take the year 1909-

speechtext: Order. I must call the hon. member's attention to the ruling of the Chair given just a few moments ago, to the effect that the debate must be relevant to the clause under consideration. Is there to be an increase in postal rates on catalogues issued by wholesale houses and departmental stores?
Mr. BURRELL.: That question does not. properly come under the present clause, and perhaps my hon. friend will refer to it again. I may say in passing that the present rate covers catalogues fairly well; it is one cent for two ounces, or eight cents per pound.

I would ask the minister if due consideration has been given to the fact that express companies are to-day' doing a good deal of business formerly done by the Post Office Department. Will not this increase in registration have a tendency to assist the express

companies in diverting moTe of the business from the Post Office Department to themselves? speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: My hon. friend knows that so far as the carrying of letters is concerned the Post Office Department is the only medium that can be employed. If I understand his question, it is whether, if this registration fee is increased, express companies, will do business by transmitting money. I could not express .an opinion on that question .offhand, but I shall consider it.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
This clause has nothing to do with catalogues. I have already

explained why it is thought desirable to increase the registration fee bringing it to exactly the same point that now obtains in the United States. I understand from the department that the present rate on catalogues is sufficiently high to fairly well cover the cost, it being eight cents a pound. In respect to what my hon friend says about the registration rate falling on the poorer people, the increased rate only falls on those who have money to send and the department has had no objection raised although this Bill has been printed for a long time.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 3-Rate on newspapers issued less frequently than monthly increased from 1 to 2 cents per pound; provision respecting circular area of 80 miles omitted; Postage rate on newspapers published oftener than _ once a week increased from J to 1 cent on and after 1st January, 1921, and after 1st January, 1922 to 1£ cents:

Before this clause carries, and I presume it will, I would like to offer a few remarks on the question of newspaper postage. We have had to-night a number of statements which I think have appealed to the members of the House and among others there was one made by the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Le-mieux) that 'the public is "plastered with taxes". My experience would lead me to the conclusion that the biggest plaster that is placed on the public at the present day is the tax that the people are required to pay in order to give our daily newspapers almost free transportation through the mails. It is a plaster of such proportions that I find it requires about $3,500,000 a yeaT to carry the daily papers of this country over and above the revenue derived from them. When we have such a plaster placed on the people I think we may well consider whether it should not be removed, and I presume the Government had in mind the removal of that plaster when they introduced {his Bill.
The deficit, as I said, on account of the newspapers is enormous. At the present time it is nothing more nor less than a method of subsidizing the newspapers, a subsidy such as no other enterprise in the country enjoys. It is a subsidy which, to my mind, cannot be justified at the present day. The financial situation of the country cannot permit it to continue.
While the hon. member for Maisonneuve criticised the department for the increased cost of the administration of the department, the House-not the department-is on 'trial in considering this bill by which. The department proposes increasing the rate on second-class matter from J cent a pound to 1 cent a pound. The House is on trial now because the House must decide whether that increase shall be made or not. If the House does not agree to increase the rate it must take the blame for continuing a very considerable portion of the present deficit in the Post Office Department.
In order that the House may more clearly understand what this means I want to give a few figures regarding some of the newspapers, because time will not permit me to take up all. I think it was the hon. member for Maisonneuve who, the other night, spoke of the newspapers being the medium for the conveyance of free thought. It occurs to me, after looking into this matter that what the newspapers are more concerned about than the carrying of free thought is free transportation, and in order to prove that and to let the House understand how much concerned they are in free transportation I propose giving some figures. I am going to jefer to only a few papers in this statement, those of Montreal, Ottawa and Toronto.
I find that at the present time the Mont* real Daily Star is paying into the Post Office Department for the carriage of that paper through the mails $24,086 per year. If they were paying 1% cents which this Bill proposes levying on newspapers after January 1922, they would on their present circulation pay about $144,000 per year. No person claims that the cent and a half tax will pay the full cost of transmission of these papers through the mail. It will not nearly pay the cost of transmission. If the higher rates suggested in this Bill were in force the Montreal Star would at the present time be paying $144,000 instead of $24,000, or it would be paying nearly $120,000 more than it is. The country is subsidizing the Montreal - Star to the extent of $120,000 a year for the despatch of their product through the mails and to their customers. Let us take another paper. The Parliament of Canada recognized, as I believe most intelligent citizens recognize, that the press of the country has an important educative influence on the entire people; and that very important fact having been recognized, a low rate was extended to all newspapers for carrying them throughout the country. Now, if the newspapers had taken advantage of that low rate and charged a high price for the papers there might be some justification for the position which the hon. member for South Perth took this evening. We delivered the papers and collected the money, and I may say incidentally that we lost a large sum in the collection, because it is a very difficult matter to collect. But that policy has prevailed for the last twenty or thirty years. The newspapers never make a dollar. Now, after that policy has been pursued all these years, adopted by successive governments as a great benefit to the people, it is now proposed to increase the rate, at one fell swoop, by 300 per cent now, and by 500 per cent a little later on. I appeal to hon. gentlemen, surely that is not a wise course to take. If you take it, then you say that the policy pursued for the last quarter of a century was a wrong one. berta and Saskatchewan some sixty newspapers large and small. These newspapers are required by the railways to pay $ 1.2b a hundredweight to take their unprinted paper into their teritory.
