I would ask the hon. member for Springfield if that is a fair deal. I do not think he will reply because I know he is too fair to say that it is. It is anything but fair.
The hon. member for Springfield told us in what a wonderful way the newspapers have been working and how he had worked hard and given something for nothing. I am glad to hear it, because we do not generally get something for nothing.
Those papers in Alberta, paying a $1.25 for their freight, and paying for their inks, are obliged to compete with newspapers delivered for twenty-five cents per hundred' weight. That is something that should be considered as against the dollar now proposed by the Government.
There is another feature. The hon. member for Springfield told us that he was selling his newspaper below cost. That is one of my causes of complaint against him. The member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) spoke to us the other night about dumping. One of my causes of complaint is the policy pursued by certain newspapers in respect to my own town. A newspaper in Hamilton sells in that city for $3.60 a year. The same newspaper, delivered practically free of charge by this Government, is sold to me in St. Catharines for $2 a year.
At the present time?

That is the latest information I have. At -any rate that was the relative price, whether it is the price now or not. When that paper sold at $2 in St. Catharines it sold at $3.60 in Hamilton. That is correct. Now I do not think that is fair.
I do not think so.

Now I want to give a quotation in order to show hon. members that all the newspapers of Canada are not agreed on this matter. The member for Lethbridge (Mr. Buchanan) the other night told us of the meeting of the Press Association, and while I know he did not want- to misinform the House still he led it to believe- and no doubt a great many of the members did believe-that the result of a meeting

which he attended represented the concensus of opinion of the whole of the newspapers of the country. But there is a difference of opinion on the matter, and I want to read something from a western paper, one that I received recently, regarding the postal rates, and this is it:
T. N. Miller of the Moose Jaw Times proposed, and L. Dalberthonson of Chauvin, Alta., seconded the following resolution, which was carried:
"Whereas the Post Office Department of Canada has under consideration an increase in the second class postal rates, and whereas it is shown that the present flat rate of 1 cent per pound for newspapers and periodicals entails a serious annual loss to the department;
"Be it resolved that the Saskatchewan Division of the Canadian Press Association place itself on record as favouring an increase in postal rates on newspapers based on the cost of transportation and based on keeping in mind the relation between the rate on newspapers and periodicals and other second-class matter transported and distributed by the Post Office Department.
"Second, that in arriving at a rate for newspaper postage the principle of the zone system should be adopted as the most equitable basis, which principle was approved by resolution of the Canadian Press Association and Canadian Press, Limited, in 1913, and that equitable rates for the zones be fixed in order that newspapers in smaller communities shall not be subject to discriminating transportation and distribution charges favourable to publications in larger centres

a discrimination in rates that results in an annual deficit for the Post Office Department.
I now wish to quote a line or two from a newspaper nearer home to further show that the feeling is not all on one side on this matter, but that there is a difference of view among the newspapers in regard to it. The St. Catharines Standard, in its issue of March 4,. 1920, states:
The smaller city dailies expect no 'favours from the Government, but they have a perfect and unassailable right to protest against a bonus being continued to newspapers in low postal rates costing the country millions of dollars annually and which works out to their own injury and ultimate destruction in many cases.
In the same editorial the Standard also says:
The Toronto papers are not ashamed to take advantage of this bonus to sell their papers at a lower price by mail, in competition with the smaller dailies, than they ask from any other class of their readers. The Globe, for instance, which preaches daily against customs tariffs and bounties, receives without protest or reproach a practical bonus from the country to assist it in its ruinous competition with the smaller city dailies.
What about the Mail and Empire?

The Mail and Empire is in exactly the same class.
An horn. MEMBER: Protection.
I am not mentioning the Mail and Empire, or the Globe, in particular. In this matter one is on the same footing as the other.
They preach different doctrines, though.
Oh, oh.
Not from Hades, I hope?

I could speak of " an
hon. gentleman angularly across the chamber," but that is too long an expression to use. I did not mean the expression that some hon. gentlemen by their laughter indicate that they know very well.

How do you yourself
know?

I have this to say, be- '
cause I do not want to take up any more time of the committee.
Go on.

I merely want to say
that I hope the minister will not recede one particle from his original resolution. I am sorry to have to say that I will not support anything but the resolution nor any amendments of the kind that have been proposed.

I merely wish to call attention to the fact that paragraph 2 deals with local papers; and I was surprised indeed to hear the remarks of my good friend from Brome (Mr. McMaster) who seemed not to be aware that local papers in his own province had been car-

ried free of charge by the Post Office Department.
It should not be. It is unbusinesslike.

That may be so, but before I get through with what I have to say the hon. gentleman may change his mind, because, the local papers that are distributed in his district are most anxious to have that state of affairs continue.
I trust the hon. member will not imply that my view on a public question is going to be influenced by the effect it will have on a newspaper in my constituency. I hope not.

I have
no doubt that is quite right so far as the hon. gentleman is concerned. I merely wish to call the attention of the committee to this fact. In 1918, we had 1,018 local weekly papers having a circulation of from 2,000 to 3,000 within a radius of forty to fifty miles. To-day we have 110 fewer of these newspapers. Conditions that have existed in these local districts have driven 110 out of existence. In the county of Lambton we had 15 local papers five years ago; 7 of these have gone out of existence. I do not need to tell hon. members what the local paper means to the district in which it is published; I have not time to tell them of the many advantages which result to the people, especially in the rural districts, through the circulation of these papers. My good friends who live in the western provinces will specially appreciate their value. In Prince Edward Island the local papers all have a circulation of over 2-,000. The bulk of the local papers in practically all the eastern provinces have a circulation of over 2,000, and the same is true of the larger number of the papers in the province of Quebec. This clause limits free distribution to those local papers which have circulations of 1,000 or less. Practically all the local papers in the following towns in Ontario have a circulation of over 2,000: Cornwall, Renfrew, Pembroke, Picton, Osh-awa, Petrolia, Arnprior, Dunnville, Am-herstburg,, Simcoe, Glencoe, -Strathroy, Leamington, Barrie, Orillia, Walkerton, Tillsonburg, Acton, Grimsby, Paris, and I could name others. Practically all the papers in these towns 'have a circulation of between 2,000 and 2,500. I urge the minister to increase that figure of 1,000 to 2,500.
Just a word with regard to the magazines. The magazines and the weekly papers 
should receive different treatment from that accorded to the daily papers. The magazines are doing a splendid work in the education of our people along the lines of the development of science, industry, trade, and so on. I hope that the minister will take into consideration the advisability of placing them at least on the half-cent basis. Even that is an increase of one hundred per cent, but I believe it would be in the best interests of the people as a whole to place the magazines in that position. As to the dailies, I do not agree with hon. gentlemen who say that the last pqnny should be exacted from them in connection with the position that they are in today. I believe that we should increase gradually our demands on the dailies from year to year. The first increase that we make upon these dailies should not exceed three-quarters of a cent per pound, payable in 11921; subsequent increases could be made later. I hope that the min- -ister will accede to the requests that I have made.
Mr. MteMASTER:	The principle that
should guide us in dealing with this question is that the papers, no matter what their circulation or the area of their distribution, should all be obliged to pay a fair consideration for the public services which they use, and that they should be brought to that position as quickly as is compatible with giving them a fair chance, having in mind the fact that they are moving from an uneconomic condition to an economic condition. To my mind, to carry mail matter of any sort free is absolutely unbusinesslike and unreasonable. Everybody should pay, but as we are trying to mend an old-established condition we should mend it in such a way as not to work harm to these people, who have been the beneficiaries or, perhaps, the victims of the condition in the past.

We have heard something about the necessity of making the newspapers pay carriage charges and about the necessity of having the increase in those charges imposed gradually.
I think there is something to be said in favour of both suggestions. It might be well to make a more gradual increase than is provided for, though I think the increase is not so very abrupt as some people would make it appear. How would it do to make an immediate increase to one-half cent per pound and then make a further increase later, say January first, to three-quarters of a cent per pound?
The increase does not take effect until next January.

I am satisfied with the suggestion that it begin next January, but the increase to one-half cent per pound might begin at once, the three-quarter cent rate become effective in January, and the rate be gradually brought up until we feel we are on safe ground. I cannot agree with my hon. friend (Mr. Mc-Master) that local papers should receive exactly the same treatment as the big dailies which are carried hundreds of thousands of miles.
, Mr. McMASTER:	I did not make any
such statement; I said that they should pay a fair price in proportion to the public service of which they avail themselves.
I accept my hon. friend's statement, although it is rather a reconstruction of what he said.

No, that is what I
said.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member
(Mr. L. Thomson) has not directly accepted the statement of the member for Brome (Mr. McMaster). I think it should be accepted absolutely.

All right, I accept it. I had a letter from a newspaper man in a town of 1,000 inhabitants who was rather surprised to find that his paper had a circulation of over 1,000. He suggested that to limit that exemption to one thousand would be placing a premium on incompetence.
If a newspaper in a little town of 1,000 inhabitants can have over 1,000 of a circulation, there is something in that objection. Either the suggestion of the hon. member for East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) should be accepted and the number w'hich will be exempted increased to 2,000 or 2,500-I am not suggesting what the number should be -or the first 1,000 should be exempted, if the matter can be arranged in that way, and then the newspapers should be allowed to pay whatever shall be agreed upon on the number over that 1,000. Either of those suggestions should be adopted by the minister, and it would be well also to adopt the suggestion which has been very generally made, that the increase in daily papers be a little more gradual.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
It has, of course, been of value to listen to the discussion and the various suggestions expressed by members
on both sides of the House, and I am not going to elaborate on any of those arguments. Before I move the amendment I am now going to move, I may say that since the Bill was published we have had views presented to this department from all parts of the country, and the department has given them all possible consideration with a view of doing what was right and just, so far as the department and officials concerned can see the whole question. First, to deal with subclause (2) of clause 3, the department recognised that it would perhaps be a hardship to limit that free circulation which I think was given first by Sir William Mulock, which, at least, has been given for a good many years, and to say to a paper that has a circulation of 1,500 or 2,000 or 2,100: You shall not enjoy that freedom at all. That would put a large number of struggling weekly papers in the country, doing a great deal of good, out of existence. Therefore, I am going to move an amendment along the line suggested by my hon friend (Mr. Armstrong). I move:
That subclause (2) of clause 3 be struck out and the following clause inserted in lieu thereof:
"Newspapers and periodicals published not more frequently than once a week in any city, town or village which has a population of not more than ten thousand persons-
That is instead of 5,000 as the subclause reads at present.
__shall be entitled to be transmitted by mail
free of postage to the extent of a circulation of 2,500 copies per issue within a distance of forty miles from their place of publication.
I might say in reference to this, that the whole plan was designed to stop what was manifestly an abuse, namely, a free circulation of weekly newspapers of big cities, which newspapers were in a prosperous condition. A weekly newspaper published in a city like Montreal or Toronto could be despatched free within a radius of forty miles. In Toronto, a newspaper could choose the zone between Toronto and Hamilton and despatch absolutely free through Toronto and Hamilton the issue of a big weekly paper, thus imposing an unnecessary burden upon the country. I think this amendment will meet the situation very well.
What was the circulation before that was allowed?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
No circulation was
mentioned. The circulation in the Bill as printed is 1,000. It has been brought to the attention of the department that in various

cities in Ontario and some further East and elsewhere the circulation of a weekly newspaper may go to 2,000 or 2,500 or 3,000, and we thought that a weekly newspaper with a larger circulation could well afford to pay.	[DOT]
The minister has increased the limit of population of a village from 5,000 to 10,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: Yes.

I do not like to
oppose the minister's view, but that seems to be aggravating the former position. There have been expressed in this House views which have impressed me, to the effect that it is not fair that any publication whatever should get off absolutely free; that the transportation facilities of the country should be placed at their disposal without any charge whatever. Notwithstanding that, we find that the limit of population is increased from 5,000 to 10,000, and if a wrong existed before, this amendment, in my judgment, is increasing the wrong.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
I do not think my hon. friend understands the situation. The question of population was never mentioned before. When this provision was inserted in the original Act, it was designed to help a number of the smaller rural papers of the country ; but under the wording of the Act, any weekly newspaper, no matter whether . it was published in a city of 500,000, would get free postage. This eliminates all that, and these papers which stand on a good footing and can well afford to pay, will have to pay, and even in smaller towns of 5,000 or 10,000 population, if weekly newspapers have a circulation of more than 2,500, they have to pay on that issue. It leaves the small weekly newspaper struggling along with the privileges it has always had.
Mr. MoMASTER: There is supposed to be a principle upon which the public life of this country should be conducted, and that is: "Equal justice for all and special privileges for none." This amendment aggravates the viciousness of the proposal contained in the Bill. It is not right to subsidize a paper because it happens to be published in a city or town or village with a population under 10,000 and because it has a circulation of under 2,500. To do that means to say that A, in a town of say 9,000 conducting a paper with a circulation of 2,300 will get his paper carried for nothing, while B in the next town, which has a population of 12,000 publishing a newspaper with 
a circulation of 2,700 will have to pay the rate that other papers are paying. That is wrong in principle, and I protest against it, and I purpose voting against the amendment.	.

My hon. friend (Mr. McMaster) has evidently never lived in a small town or he would not speak as he has done. These local papers are delivered free in that town and in the surrounding country to a very large extent. They are placed in the post office and simply handed out by the postmaster, or they are sent out to the rural routes for miles and miles around that little town. When the hon. gentleman talks aljout an expense on the Post Office Department, he is entirely wrong.
If the papers are carried by the rural route for miles and miles around the town, that costs the people of Canada something.
All right.	'

Following the principle laid down by my hon. friend (Mr. McMaster), if there be a principle involved, that all of these newspapers must pay for the service they are receiving-
Mr. MoMASTER: That is the principle we should try to adopt.
Mr. NICHOLSON (Algoma) -then the large daily newspapers would have to pay, as the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Chaplin) has stated, six or seven cents a pound. If we are going to carry the principle to its logical conclusion and tax the paper that is carried forty miles and no further, what the service is worth, then we must go back and tax the paper that is carried 500 or 600 or 2,000 or 3,000 miles in proportion, and we shall have to work out a tariff rate just the same as you have for other commodities.
Why not?

It is too
late to go into that argument row; but we are dealing with the question when we are simply charging a daily paper a small portion of what it is costing to carry the daily paper. If we are going to let the daily paper off with five, or four, or three cents a pound on any quantity whatever when we are carrying it any distance from forty miles up to three thousand miles, surely it is fair to give some advantage to the weekly paper that is circulated within forty miles. On the larger question my own

opinion is that it is very doubtful whether the Parliament of Canada should undertake to create a tariff on newspa/pers through which the people of this country, particularly in the remote sections, get their ideas-whether correct or not I am not going to discuss-just the same as upon any other commodity. It is a question whether it is not in the interests of the people to make it easy for the newspapers to get into circulation. There is a limit beyond which you cannot go. As to the small newspaper, if we are going to make1 a concession to the larger newspaper such as this Bill proposes, surely the small newspaper is entitled to some concession, and you cannot give them any concession under the present proposal unless you give them the 40-mile zone the minister provides for in this Bill.

This has been a very enlightening discussion indeed, and though the hour is getting early (I think we are justified in spending a few more moments on it, although I shall not detain the House more than a few minutes. I agree for once with the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) -and11 believe it is the first time I have the privilege of agreeing with any principle laid down by the hon. member in financial matters,-that every public service that is rendered by this Government, whether by the railways, ships, post office, telegraph, or telephone, if we own one, should at least be self-sustaining. I have made an appeal in this House on two or three occasions this session to have the railway rates, both passenger and freight, advanced, although it would mean a considerably increased expenditure to some concerns in which I am interested. 1 have made that appeal at least twice, but apparently it has fallen on deaf ears so far. I hope it may bear fruit some day. It has been generally contended here to-night that we are subsidizing the press of Canada to the amount of about $5,000,000 per annum. I have heard my friends opposite talk about a subsidized press in this country a good many times, and I always thought they were wrong when they used that word1, but now after hearing what has been said to-night as to the way we are carrying the newspapers over this country I feel they are right. I do not like to offend my good friend from Springfield (Mr. Richardson), who is a newspaper man. but I think that in asking that this rate be only 1 cent he is asking for too much of a reduction.

What would you
suggest?

I think this advance should have gone into effect at least five years ago. We shall only be catching up a very small proportion of what we have lost in the last five or ten years. Notice is given that the new rates will not become operative until January next.
Make it retroactive.

My friend suggests
that the rate should be made retroactive. That would not please my hon. friend from Springfield and other hon. gentlemen. As a matter of ordinary business the rates should have been advanced long ago. There is no doubt that this country has lost almost a score of million dollars within the last few years through not changing the rate. We have taxed every conceivable thing lately, and for some of the taxes we pay we get no service at all. Take the luxury tax that has just been proposed, and the income tax. The money is taken but no service whatever is rendered. The same is- true of the business tax. Now here we have a big service rendered at a price of not more than ten or fifteen per cent of its cost. Surely under those conditions it is not wise to ask that this Government should continue that rate for a moment longer than is necessary, although, -of course, fair notice should be given to the press. Many of the newspapers are good friends of mine. I do not grumble about the press abusing me. I get "bouquets" sometimes, it is true; perhaps II deserve them; we have all to take our bumps. II have not got up in this House in the last five years to complain of anything the press has said of me, not even the Western press. Some of the criticisms come by letter and others by newspaper. That is all right. I let them pass.
I	think the press does not always give the best education that it might give, but my views may be wrong. I do not like the unsigned editorial; I never did. A good many people read an editorial and think that is public opinion. It is not public opinion at all. It is the opinion of one man, and he is often paid to write a certain class of article which would often be very different if he were writing his own views. It is only the opinion of one man, and he may not be the best class of man even at that.
There is one point that has not been brought out, and as to which I should like the minister to give me some information. I want to know if the minister has taken into account the amount we get from the American newspaper that is published over the border -and that circulates in vast num-

bers through our part of the country? What proportion of the postage on American, papers coming into Canada goes into the coffers of the people of Canada? I see some of my friends shaking their heads. I suppose we get it all, then. The papers from Buffalo come into our town, very freely. I presume they pay a very low rate in Buffalo. I want to know from the minister how much of that revenue that is paid to the United States postal department comes into the coffers of the Canadian Government. I think it will be found that we are carrying American newstpapens on our side of the line and making delivery of them at rates that we are denying to our own Canadian papers. If that is so, ilt is a false situation, and some corrective means should be found. I suppose the answer will be that we are in a postal union with the United States, and that they make a collection on their side and possibly pay us a small amount. I do not know whether the minister is paying attention to this question, but I would ask him what portion of the postage on American papers coming into Canada goes into the coffers of our Post Office Department?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: None of it, I am infoamed, unless they happen to be re-mailed in Canada. It is the same with our papers on the other side of the line.

I have sat quiet
for the last three or four weeks when the Budget proposals were being discussed, so I am going to talk for a few minutes now. I regret that we have not heard from the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) on this question. He is a distinguished journalist and a man of very wide experience, and I would sit as one at the feet of Gamaliel if he were to speak on this question.
Would you profit as much as did the apostle?

Seeing that it is
not the hon, member for Brome, I think I would derive some profit. I did not quite appreciate a remark that the minister made with regard to these weekly papers. He justified the carrying of these papers free at public expense on the ground that they did a great deal of good. I think that remark tends to discriminate against the daily paper. I hesitate to spring into the field in defence of the daily paper, but I want to say as a journalist of some experience, if the weekly paper does a great deal of good, what about the great daily news-

paper? One hon. gentleman says they do a great deal of harm. I do not think so. A great modem daily newspaper, with the news of the world dished up in acceptable form, and with those features that appeal to different classes of the public, its family section, its illustrations, and its funny pictures, and so forth, must perforce be of vast benefit to the'people of this country, and we have many such great dailies in Canada. I do not wish to plead this case unduly, but it does seem to me that the argument in favour of a gradual increase iis one that the minister ought nolt to resist. I think that in time-it need not be too long-the newspapers perhaps should pay the cost of transportation, but to press the whole burden on them at once seems to me to be an unwise proceeding.
Before I sit down I want to say, after listening to the debates for the last few weeks, that all this talk about 'taxation, and taxation, and taxation, has been getting on my nerves; and it does seem to me that after having imposed taxation on pretty nearly everything we eat and wear it will undoubtedly perplex and irritate a great section of the country if undue taxation is now placed upon the newspapers.
Mr. DuTREMBLAY: lit seems to me that
the increase proposed is too sudden. Newspapers have been subscribed for for a year or two at a certain rate,-$3 or $3.60 per annum, as the case may be, dependent on what they have to pay to the Government for transmission. Resides increased wages the newspapers have to contend now with an increase in the price of newsprint; I understand that the cost of paper is more than double what it was at the outbreak of the war, and. the newspapers were certainly not contemplating such a drastic proposal- as this. To ask them to pay an increase from a quarter of a cent to a cent is, I think, unfair, and the Government should show some sense of justice in this matter; I do not -think they are justified in taking the people by the throat, and as the newspapers have no means of increasing their rates so far as subscriptions already taken in are concerned,, this increase will mean a big loss to those papers. I think, therefore, that the minister would do well to consider the representations that have been made by those hon. members who have advocated a moderate course. A few moments -ago I listened to the remarks of the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt). Whenever there is a question of tariff under consideration

that. hon. gentleman is always anxious that we should go slow, and I am sure that if the newspaper business were near his heart he would ask the Government to go slow and slower.

The hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Richardson) having been kind enough to refer to me, I feel it incumbent on me to say something on the subject, although I do not feel, justified at this date hour in making any extended remarks in regard to the usefulness of the press. Where an established privilege has'been granted in the past, even though improvidently, any drastic change is always objectionable. I agree that the newspapers should contribute more liberally than they have done in the past to the revenue of the country, in view of the many claims which are now being made on the public treasury; and I concur with the minister in his desire to get extra revenue. But I think he should obtain that revenue by gradual means and not by any precipitate measure. That, briefly,, is the view I wish to express on this subject.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
I move that after the
word "week" in the twenty-seventh line ^of clause 3, subclause (3) the following words be inserted:
-and the newspapers and periodicals described in the immediately preceding subsection upon any copies in excess of the circulation of 2,5'00 copies.
I move to amend the clause further by striking out the words "one cent" in the twenty-eighth line and substituting Ithe words "three quarters of a cent." In reference to this second amendment, I have listened carefully to Ithe arguments advanced on both sides of the House to-night, and I may say that the department has had during the last two or three weeks an enormous number of representations on the subject. Views have been expressed from all sources along various lines, and although I still believe that the principle of trying to gelt the people to pay for public service is right, I am prepared to make a concession. However, in spite of the protests that have been made by the press that they should nolt be compelled to pay more than half a cent a pound at this time, so that they may adjust themselves at a latter date to a higher figure, I do not think that they should continue at the present rate of a quarter of a cent; nor should we accept the suggestion of half a cent. The least we ought to accept is three-quarters of a cent, which is a compromise
that might at all events be fairly satisfactory to those who hold strong views on either side of the question. At present they are paying a quarter of a cent, and this will make Ithem pay three-quarters, and we propose to leave in the Bill the provision as it stands to make this double on the first of January, 1922. Whatever burden this may be on the people, and however much we may sympathize wilth the condition in regard to the shortage of newsprint, I think it will be conceded that this proposal is a fair compromise.

When we realize how much the country is contributing for the transmission of papers through the mail, it seems to me that it is not unreasonable to ask that ithe newspapers should pay one cent a pound, because that does not come near to meeting the cost of their transmission. I appreciate all that has been said in regard Ito the difficulties which the newspapers are up against. Every one of us has encountered such difficulties. I have had to contend *with difficulties in my business, and I think that every man in this House has had to do the same. But we have had ito adjust our business to changed conditions, and I see no Teason why an exception should be made of newspapers at the present time. I do not think that the amendment should carry.

speechtext:
Amendments agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 4-Certain letters and other mailable matter to be free of postage.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
I move that section 4
be amended by substituting for the new section 75 as printed in the Bill the following :
75. All letters and other mailable matter sent, at the seat of government, by the Governor General, by any minister, by any department of the Government, by the office of the Auditor General, or by the Librarians of Parliament, shall be free of Canada postage under such regulations as are from time to time made in that respect by the Governor in Council; and the provisions of any other statute inconsistent with the provisions of this Act, or conferring on any person or body greater powers of sending or having sent mailable matter free of postage than are conferred by this Act, shall be hereafter construed as conferring on such person or body no other or greater privileges than are conferred by this Act upon the persons and departments hereinbefore named.
Some bodies, like the Railway Commission, Civil Service Commission and Soldiers' Settlement Board have been given special powers with regard to the franking

privilege greater than are given under this section. As the section read they would have had greater franking privileges given them than are given by this Bill. This really means that boards and commissions which have been given the statutory authority to use the franking privilege shall have no greater powers than are conferred by this Act.
Why not set them forth as you do the others?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: This was gone into by the Parliamentary Counsel and he has given it a great deal of thought.

This is a mysterious thing. The ordinary wayfaring man will not know who is entitled to the franking privilege. I think we ought to know. I do not see why each of these departments should not be mentioned. Why should not the public know who has the franking privilege?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: I do not know that there will be any disadvantage in it and there may be some advantage. Of course they are all given this privilege by statute.
I cannot see why one department is mentioned and the other is not. I cannot understand the logic of it.
Is there any department struck off that has the franking privilege?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
